topics.name: Indefinite Integration
topics.line: Reverse differentiation: know the standard list, then the substitution and parts.

sections.ti: Integration as the reverse of differentiation, and the constant of integration
sections.tx: Integration is just differentiation run backwards — you are handed the derivative and asked for the function — and since a constant dies on differentiating, every answer carries a + c.
sections.slip: Writing ∫(2x + 1/x)dx = x² + ln x and stopping there. Always add + c. The function it came from could have had any constant attached, because the constant disappears on differentiating. Without c your answer is only one member of the family. Thinking a function has one single integral, the way it has one single derivative. Differentiation gives one answer; integration gives infinitely many, all differing by a constant. x² + ln x + 50 and x² + ln x + 200 are equally correct. Reading ∫aˣ ln a dx = aˣ + c and then writing ∫aˣ dx = aˣ · ln a + c. ln a was multiplying inside the integral, so it comes out as a divisor: ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + c. Divide, never multiply.

sections.ti: Splitting with 1 − sin²x: the add-and-subtract trick
sections.tx: When cos²x sits on top of (1 + x²)sin²x, write cos²x = 1 − sin²x — the fraction splits into cosec²x − 1/(1 + x²) and integrates to −cot x − tan⁻¹x + C.
sections.slip: Writing cos²x = 1 + sin²x instead of 1 − sin²x. The sign slips out easily and it is just as easy to miss. sin²x + cos²x = 1, so cos²x = 1 − sin²x. The 1 loses sin²x, it never gains it. Check the sign out loud before you split. Splitting the fraction straight away, before the numerator has 1 + x² in it. Then nothing cancels and you are stuck with a messier integral than you started with. Fix the numerator first, then split. The split is the last step, not the first. Dropping a minus sign at the end and writing cot x + tan⁻¹x. ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x, and the second term already came with its own minus. Both minus signs stay: −cot x − tan⁻¹x + C.

sections.ti: Linear upon linear: adjusting powers to substitute (x+2)/(x−1)
sections.tx: When a fourth root hides (x−1)³(x+2)⁵, balance the two powers so that a linear upon linear becomes t — and it does not matter which of the two you call t, both roads land on the same answer.
sections.slip: Raising the power of one linear without compensating. Students write (x−1)⁸ and forget the ((x+2)/(x−1))⁵ that pays for it. Whatever power you write below, write the same power above. (x−1)³(x+2)⁵ = (x−1)⁸ · ((x+2)/(x−1))⁵ — multiply it back once in your head and the identity is obvious. The sign slip at the last step: carrying −(1/3) and dividing by −(1/4), then writing −(4/3). Minus into minus is plus. −(1/3) ÷ (−1/4) = +4/3. Write the two minus signs out, don't do it mentally. Thinking your answer is wrong because the printed one looks different, with (x−1)/(x+2) instead of (x+2)/(x−1). Flip the fraction and flip the sign of the power: ((x+2)/(x−1))^(−1/4) = ((x−1)/(x+2))^(1/4). Same answer, different dress.

sections.ti: Linear upon quadratic, and the sin inverse homework question
sections.tx: Linear upon quadratic = (derivative of the quadratic) + constant, and the same eye for "what is the top the derivative of?" turns ∫ sin x dx/√(sin²x − sin²α) into a plain sin⁻¹ form with cos x = t.
sections.slip: Substituting cos x = t and writing sin x dx = dt, so the minus sign vanishes. Differentiate out loud: cos x = t gives −sin x dx = dt, so sin x dx = −dt. Write that line before you touch the integral. Trying to push √(sin²x − sin²α) straight into the a² − x² format while the top is sin x dx. It is not a² − x² in sin x. Convert sin²x to 1 − cos²x and sin²α to 1 − cos²α first; then the denominator is cos²α − cos²x and the substitution is obvious. Treating α as a variable and trying to differentiate sin²α or tan²α. In these questions α is fixed. sin²α, cos²α, tan²α are all constants — only x is integrated.

sections.ti: Partial fractions: splitting a fraction into smaller ones
sections.tx: A proper fraction with distinct linear factors splits as A/(x−a₁) + B/(x−a₂) + C/(x−a₃); cross-multiply, put each root one by one to get A, B, C, and the integral is just logs.
sections.slip: Splitting without checking that the fraction is proper. First compare powers. The numerator's power must be less than the denominator's. If it is not, divide first, then split the leftover fraction. Putting x = 1, 2, 3 into the original fraction instead of the cross-multiplied identity. Those values make the denominator zero. Always cross-multiply first, get the polynomial identity, and substitute into that. Writing ln(x−2) without the modulus. Every piece integrates to a log of the modulus: ln|x−2|. Make it a habit, it is a free mark lost otherwise.

sections.ti: Practice Set: Five By-Parts Problems with Hints
sections.tx: Five by-parts questions to attempt yourself — at least three, with only the first move given: multiply x/(1+sin x) by 1 − sin x, split sec³x as sec x·sec²x, and substitute t = 1/x before you part cos(1/x)/x³.
f: $$\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\cdot\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x} = \frac{x(1-\sin x)}{\cos^{2}x} = x\sec^{2}x - x\sec x\tan x$$
sections.slip: Starting by parts on x/(1+sin x) exactly as it is written, taking u = x and the whole 1/(1+sin x) as the other part. You cannot integrate 1/(1+sin x) comfortably, so you are stuck before you start. Rationalise with 1 − sin x first; only then pick u and v. Forgetting that substitution exists and attacking cos(1/x)/x³ directly with by parts. Put t = 1/x first. The question becomes −∫ t cos t dt, and then by parts takes one line. In sec³x, splitting correctly but then differentiating sec²x and integrating sec x. Integrate the easy half. ∫sec²x dx = tan x is instant, so sec²x is the part you integrate and sec x is the part you differentiate.

sections.ti: Using the x f′ Form: ∫(ln(ln x) + 1/ln x)dx
sections.tx: If the question gives you f(x) but not its partner x·f′(x), write the partner in yourself and subtract it the same line — then check whether the leftover is itself an f + x f′ pair.
sections.slip: Comparing f′ with the question instead of x·f′, and concluding the form does not fit. For f = ln(ln x), f′ = 1/(x ln x) but x·f′ = 1/ln x. Always multiply by x first; that is what you must hunt for in the question. Adding 1/ln x to make the pattern and forgetting to subtract it. You cannot add a term free of cost. Write + 1/ln x and − 1/ln x together in the same step, before doing anything else. Getting x·ln(ln x) and then treating the leftover as a new, hard integral. Test the leftover for the same form. Take g = 1/ln x, build x·g′, and you will see the leftover is already a g + x·g′ pair.

sections.ti: Numerator = λ·Denominator + μ·(Derivative of Denominator) [+ γ]
sections.tx: When the numerator is the troublemaker, write it as λ(denominator) + μ(derivative of denominator) + γ, and the integral falls apart into λx + μ ln|denominator| + γ∫dx/denominator.
f: $$p\sin x + q\cos x + r = \lambda\,(a\sin x + b\cos x + c) + \mu\,(a\cos x - b\sin x) + \gamma$$
$$\int \frac{dx}{a\sin x + b\cos x + c}\ \text{with}\ t = \tan\frac{x}{2},\ \sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^{2}},\ \cos x = \frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}},\ dx = \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}$$
sections.slip: Writing μ times something that is not exactly the derivative of the denominator — a sign flipped in D′, usually the −b sin x. Write D′ separately on the side, once, and check its sign before you compare anything. If D′ is wrong, the ln step is wrong and the whole answer collapses. Denominator has a constant, but you only keep λ and μ. Then your three comparisons contradict each other and you think the method failed. A constant in the denominator means one more unknown γ in the numerator. Three unknowns, three relations — sin x, cos x, and the constant term. Stopping at λx + μ ln|D| and quietly dropping the γ piece. γ∫dx/D is a full standard question on its own. Finish it with t = tan(x/2); it is the easiest part of the sum.

topics.name: Definite Integration
topics.line: Limits first, then properties that halve the work.

sections.ti: Newton–Leibniz rule: differentiating without integrating
sections.tx: To differentiate a definite integral whose limits are functions of x, put the upper limit into the function and multiply by its derivative, then subtract the same thing done with the lower limit — no integration needed.
sections.slip: Integrating first, then differentiating. You do double work and end up in the same place. Worse, in many questions the function cannot be integrated at all, and then you are stuck. Even for an easy f(t) like t³, where you do know the integral, apply the rule — it is much faster. Putting in the limits but forgetting to multiply by their derivatives. Every limit brings its own derivative as a product. sin x brings cos x, x² brings 2x. Only the plain upper limit x gets 1, which is why that factor is invisible in the special case. Getting confused by the dummy variable, or treating t as if it survives. f(t)dt, f(u)du, f(y)dy — all the same thing. After the limits go in, the dummy letter is gone and the answer is a function of x only.

sections.ti: A zero definite integral forces a crossing of the x-axis
sections.tx: If a continuous f(x) has ∫ from a to b equal to 0, the positive and negative areas have cancelled, so the graph must cross the x-axis at least once between a and b.
sections.slip: Reading ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = 0 as "f(x) = 0 everywhere on [a, b]". Zero integral means the areas cancelled, not that the function vanished. f = 0 everywhere gives integral 0, but integral 0 does not give f = 0 everywhere. Saying the graph crosses the x-axis exactly once. Claim only at least once. The cancelling can happen with many crossings; one is the minimum guaranteed. Using this result when f is not continuous. Continuity is the reason it must pass through zero. Drop continuity and the function can jump from plus to minus without ever being 0.

sections.ti: Discussion of the Laila–Majnu practice set
sections.tx: When f(x) and its partner f(a+b−x) add up to 1, the definite integral is just (upper − lower)/2 — even when the partner is hidden inside something like (6 − x)².
sections.slip: Reading a + b off the function instead of the limits. a + b comes only from the limits of integration. Here 2 + 4 = 6, so you substitute 6 − x. Trying to actually integrate x²/(x² + (6 − x)²). Don't. Indefinite integration here is a trap. Pair it with King rule, add, and the denominator cancels. Writing (upper − lower)/2 by reflex, without checking the pair. Add f(x) + f(a+b−x) first. Only when that sum is exactly 1 is the answer half the width.

sections.ti: Jack rule: odd and even functions over −a to a
sections.tx: Between −a and +a, an odd function integrates to 0 and an even function to twice its 0-to-a integral — that is Jack rule, and it falls straight out of King.
sections.slip: Writing 0 for an odd function when the limits are not of the form −a to +a, like 1 to 3 or −2 to 5. Jack needs the lower limit to be exactly the negative of the upper limit. Check the limits first, the function second. Deciding odd or even by glancing at powers, so a product like sin¹⁹x · cos¹⁵x gets called even. Actually substitute −x and simplify. Keep the combinations straight: odd × even = odd, odd × odd = even, even × even = even. Treating 2∫ from 0 to a as a final answer in the even case. In the even case only the limit changed. The integration is still pending — do it. The free answer exists only in the odd case.

sections.ti: Periodic functions in definite integration
sections.tx: If f has period T, every block of length T contributes the same integral — so count how many periods the interval is worth, integrate over one period, and multiply.
sections.slip: Taking the length of the interval as a − b instead of b − a, and getting a sign wrong. Length is always upper limit minus lower limit: b − a for a to b. Write it down as a subtraction before you touch the formula. Seeing limits mT to nT and multiplying by n. The number of periods is (n − m), not n. For 50T to 53T it is 3, not 53. Shifting the limits by an amount that is not a whole multiple of T. Only a shift of nT keeps the graph identical. If the shift is not a whole number of periods, the shape you are integrating is different and the property does not apply.

sections.ti: Newton–Leibniz rule: differentiate first, read the question later
sections.tx: If x sits in the limits of a definite integral, differentiate first with Newton–Leibniz — top limit put in place of t times its derivative, minus the same for the bottom limit — and read the question only after that.
sections.slip: Trying to actually integrate (sin t)/√t before differentiating. You can't, and you don't need to. Newton–Leibniz is a differentiation technique, not a solving technique. It hands you the derivative without ever touching the integration. Writing only the upper-limit term when the lower limit is also a function of x. In the x² to x³ question, forgetting the − (sin x²)/√(x²) × 2x piece makes the answer wrong. A constant lower limit kills that term; a variable lower limit never does. Substituting the limit but forgetting to multiply by its derivative. The chain rule factor is the whole point of the rule. x³ brings a 3x², x² brings a 2x, ln x brings a 1/x. No substitution without its derivative attached.

sections.ti: tanⁿx on 0 to π/4: Iₙ + Iₙ₊₂ = 1/(n+1)
sections.tx: For Iₙ = ∫₀^(π/4) tanⁿx dx, don't reduce — just add: Iₙ + Iₙ₊₂ = 1/(n+1), and the whole family falls out in one line.
sections.slip: Writing the answer as 1/(n+2), because the question had an n+2 in it. The n+2 is in the subscript, not in the answer. The power after integrating tⁿ is n+1, so the denominator is n+1. Sanity-check with n = 1: I₁ + I₃ must be 1/2. Trying Iₙ − Iₙ₊₂ out of habit. Subtracting leaves tanⁿx (1 − tan²x), and 1 − tan²x is nobody's derivative. The entire trick lives on 1 + tan²x = sec²x, so here you add. Seeing 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and calling them an AP because the gaps 'look' equal. 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 but 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12, so they are not in AP. For HP you must first take reciprocals: 2, 3, 4, and those are in AP.

sections.ti: Bonus: a product series via logarithms
sections.tx: A product series has no formula of its own — set it equal to λ, take ln on both sides to turn it into a sum, and ∫₀¹ 2x·ln(1+x²) dx = ln(4/e) gives λ = 4/e.
sections.slip: Searching for a direct formula for the product and losing five minutes. There is no shortcut inside a product. Convert it to a sum with log — that is the only route, and it is quick. Replacing r/n by x while a stray n is still floating around, because the 1/n was never taken out. First write the term as (1/n) × (something purely in r/n). The 1/n becomes dx; everything else becomes the function. Stopping at 2 ln 2 − 1 and writing that as the answer. That value is ln λ, not λ. Write 1 as ln e, squeeze it into one log ln(4/e), then compare with ln λ to get λ = 4/e.

topics.name: Area Under Curves
topics.line: Sketch the region, choose vertical or horizontal strips, then integrate.

sections.ti: Why area is not just definite integration
sections.tx: The length of any vertical line is y upper minus y lower, with signs, and it always comes out positive.
sections.slip: Subtracting in the order the points happen to be written, which gives a negative length. Length is never negative. Identify the upper point first, then subtract the lower one. Dropping the minus sign of a negative y coordinate — writing 1 − 7 = −6 instead of −1 − (−7) = 6. Substitute each y with its sign inside a bracket. The bracket is what saves the marks. Assuming area and the definite integral are the same thing because the formula looks familiar. Treat area as a length of a stripe added up. Get the stripe's length right, with signs, and the integral then gives the area.

sections.ti: Region between y = x² and y = −x² + 9: legs switching over
sections.tx: Where y = x² and y = 9 − x² cross at x = ±3/√2 the upper and lower legs trade places, so the vertical-stripe integral must be broken there.
sections.slip: Writing one integral from 0 to 3 with the height (9 − x²) − x² throughout. That height is only true till x = 3/√2. After that the stripe flips, so the second piece needs x² − (9 − x²). Break at the crossing. Keeping the same curve on top after the switch and getting a negative piece, then ignoring the minus sign. For a vertical stripe it is always the one above minus the one below. Test one value of x in each piece to see which curve is actually on top. Mixing up x = 3/√2 with x = 3. x = 3/√2 ≈ 2.12 is where the two curves cross each other. x = 3 is only where the downward parabola meets the x-axis. Different points, different jobs.

sections.ti: Practice: set up three regions yourself
sections.tx: Three regions, five minutes: plot each one, pick the stripe that fits, and stop the moment the integral is written.
sections.slip: Reading the three questions and nodding along without writing anything. Pen on paper for all three. This concept gets covered fast after this, and only written practice carries you forward. Rushing to a final number and leaving the setup half done. Setup first, for all three regions. The value can wait; at most do half the integration if time is left. Writing dy in the integral but keeping x limits (or the reverse). A dy integral takes y limits and the length written in y only. Check that the variable in the limits matches the differential.

sections.ti: Shade the region bounded by x² = y, x² = −y and y = 4x − 3
sections.tx: Draw x² = y and its mirror x² = −y, cut them with y = 4x − 3 to get (1,1), (3,9) and x = −2 ± √7, then shade the small middle region with horizontal stripes so one leg always stays on the line.
sections.slip: Substituting the line into x² = −y and writing x² − 4x + 3 = 0 again, by reflex. The minus sits on y, so x² = −(4x − 3) = 3 − 4x, giving x² + 4x − 3 = 0. Different equation, different roots — one factorises, the other does not. Reading x² = −y as a parabola opening to the left. x is still squared, so the axis is still vertical. Only the direction along y changes: it opens downwards. Taking a vertical stripe out of habit, then discovering halfway that the bottom leg has changed curve. Mark the switch point first — here x = −2 + √7, where the line meets the lower parabola. If a stripe changes legs, turn it ninety degrees and check the other direction before you write a single integral.

sections.ti: sin(ax) graphs by rescaling the period
sections.tx: To plot sin(ax), don't stretch or squeeze the picture — keep the same sine shape and divide every marked x-value by |a|, because period = T/|a|.
f: $$\text{if period of } f(x) = T \text{ then period of } f(ax) = \frac{T}{|a|}$$
sections.slip: Trying to squeeze or stretch the drawn curve freehand to get sin 2x or sin(x/2). Don't. Keep the same sine shape and only change the x-coordinates using period = T/|a|. It is a numbers job, not a drawing job. Multiplying the x-values by a instead of dividing, so sin 2x comes out with period 4π. The period is divided by |a|, so the marks are divided by |a| too. For a = 2, π/2 becomes π/4 — the wave gets shorter, not longer. Getting lost with a fraction like a = ½ or a = 3/2 and guessing the direction. Dividing by ½ means multiplying by 2; dividing by 3/2 means multiplying by 2/3. Do that one fraction step on paper, then apply it to every mark.

sections.ti: Graphs of sin x + cos x and |cos x − sin x| on [0°, 90°]
sections.tx: On 0 to π/2, differentiate to see sin x + cos x rise to a peak √2 at π/4 and cos x − sin x fall from 1 to −1, then open the modulus as cos x − sin x before π/4 and sin x − cos x after it.
f: $$|\cos x - \sin x| = \begin{cases} \cos x - \sin x, & 0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{4} \\ \sin x - \cos x, & \frac{\pi}{4} \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2} \end{cases}$$
sections.slip: Guessing the shape of sin x + cos x instead of differentiating it. You cannot place the peak by eye. Differentiate, solve y′ = 0 to get π/4, and check the sign of y′ on both sides. Putting the modulus on first and then trying to differentiate |cos x − sin x| in one go. Draw cos x − sin x first, find where it crosses zero, then reflect the negative part upward. Order matters. Treating the modulus graph as one single formula for the whole interval 0 to π/2. It is two different formulas joined at π/4. Write the piecewise definition on paper before you integrate, otherwise the area comes out wrong.

sections.ti: Area Common to a Circle and a Parabola
sections.tx: For the region inside both y² = 3x and x² + y² = 4, slice it with a horizontal strip: the right leg comes off the circle, the left leg off the parabola, y runs 0 to √3, and you double for symmetry.
sections.slip: Writing the strip length as parabola minus circle, and getting a negative answer. In this region the circle is always the right boundary and the parabola the left one. Length is always right minus left: √(4 − y²) − y²/3. Taking y from 0 to 2 because the circle's top is at y = 2. The strip survives only till the curves cross. Solve the two equations, get y = √3, and stop there. Forgetting the factor 2 and reporting only the upper half. Write the 2 outside the integral the moment you decide to use symmetry, not after you have evaluated.

sections.ti: Choosing x or y, and the Difference of Roots
sections.tx: Whichever variable the parabola is quadratic in, kill the other one, cube that variable's difference of roots (√D/|a| — never solve), and divide by 6 times the latus rectum.
sections.slip: Parabola is quadratic in y, but you still cube the difference of x values because that is what you did in the last question. The variable is not your choice, it is the parabola's. x = 3y² − 2y + 1 is quadratic in y, so eliminate x and use y₂ − y₁. Hunting for the actual roots of 3y² − 11y + 3 = 0 and losing two minutes in surds. You never need the roots, only their difference: √D/|a| = √85/3. Cube it and move on. Applying the formula blindly when D is negative, as in 3y² − 3y + 3 = 0, and reporting some imaginary area. Check D first. D < 0 means the line never cuts the parabola, so there is no region to find — the question itself is wrong.

questions.q: If the area of the region $\{(x,y): 0 \le y \le \frac{k}{\sqrt{x+1}}, 0 \le x \le 3\}$ is equal to 12, then the value of $k$ is:
questions.s:
Area $A = \int_0^3 \frac{k}{\sqrt{x+1}} dx = k[2\sqrt{x+1}]_0^3 = k(2\sqrt{4}-2\sqrt{1})=k(4-2)=2k$.
Given $A=12$, so $2k=12 \implies k=6$.

questions.q: The integral $\int \frac{(x^4-1)dx}{x(x^4+1)\ln(x^2+\frac{1}{x^2})}$ is equal to:
questions.s:
Let $t = \ln(x^2+1/x^2)$. Then $dt = \frac{2(x^4-1)}{x(x^4+1)}dx$.
The integral becomes $\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{dt}{t} = \frac{1}{2}\ln|t|+C$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=e^x$, $y=e^{-x}$ and the line $x=1$ is:
questions.s:
The curves intersect at $x=0$.
The region is bounded by $x=0$ and $x=1$.
Area $A = \int_0^1 (e^x - e^{-x}) dx = [e^x + e^{-x}]_0^1 = (e+e^{-1})-(1+1) = e+1/e-2$.

questions.q: If $\int \frac{dx}{a+b\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{6} \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\tan x}{3}\right)+C$ for $a,b>0$, then the area of the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a} + \frac{y^2}{b} = 1$ is:
questions.s:
The integral form is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{a(a+b)}}\tan^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{a}\tan x}{\sqrt{a+b}})$. Comparing gives $\sqrt{a(a+b)}=6$ and $\frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{a+b}}=\frac{2}{3}$.
Solving yields $a=4, b=5$.
Area is $\pi\sqrt{ab} = \pi\sqrt{20}=2\pi\sqrt{5}$.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\int \frac{\sqrt{x}}{x^{1/3}+1}dx$ and $f(0)=0$, then $f(1)$ is equal to:
questions.s:
Let $x=t^6$. The integral becomes $\int \frac{6t^8}{t^2+1}dt$.
Long division gives $\int 6(t^6-t^4+t^2-1 + \frac{1}{t^2+1})dt$.
Integrating and using $f(0)=0$ gives $f(1)=6(\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}-1+\frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{152}{35}$.

Let $I_n = \int_0^{\pi/4} \tan^n x dx$. The value of $I_8+I_6$ is:

$I_n = \int_0^{\pi/4} \tan^{n-2}x \tan^2 x dx = \int_0^{\pi/4} \tan^{n-2}x (\sec^2 x - 1) dx$

questions.q: The area of the region $\{(x,y):|x-5|\le y\le\sqrt{25-x^2}\}$ is:

This is the area of a quarter circle of radius 5, minus the area of a triangle with base 5 and height 5. $A = \frac{\pi(5^2)}{4} - \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \frac{25\pi}{4}-\frac{25}{2}$.

questions.q: If $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{n} x}{\sin^n x + \cos^n x} dx$ for any $n \in \mathbb{R}$, then the value of $I$ is:
questions.s:
Using the King's rule property $\int_0^a f(x)dx = \int_0^a f(a-x)dx$.
$I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^n(\pi/2-x)}{\sin^n(\pi/2-x)+\cos^n(\pi/2-x)}dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^n x}{\cos^n x+\sin^n x}dx$.
Adding the two expressions for $I$:
$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^n x + \cos^n x}{\sin^n x + \cos^n x} dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} 1 dx = \pi/2$.
Therefore, $I = \pi/4$.

questions.q: The value of $\int_{e^{-1}}^{e^2} \frac{|\ln x|}{x} dx$ is:
questions.s:
The function $\ln x$ is negative for $x \in (0,1)$ and positive for $x>1$.
We split the integral at $x=1$.
$I = \int_{e^{-1}}^1 \frac{-\ln x}{x} dx + \int_1^{e^2} \frac{\ln x}{x} dx$.
Let $u=\ln x$, so $du=dx/x$.
$I = -\int_{-1}^0 u du + \int_0^2 u du = -[\frac{u^2}{2}]_{-1}^0 + [\frac{u^2}{2}]_0^2 = -(0-\frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{4}{2}-0) = \frac{1}{2}+2 = \frac{5}{2}$.

questions.q: The value of $\int_{-1}^{1} (|x| + [x]) dx$, where $[x]$ is the greatest integer function, is:
questions.s:
We can split the integral: $I = \int_{-1}^1 |x|dx + \int_{-1}^1 [x]dx$.
The first part is an integral of an even function: $\int_{-1}^1 |x|dx = 2\int_0^1 x dx = 2[x^2/2]_0^1 = 1$.
The second part must be split by the definition of $[x]$: $\int_{-1}^1 [x]dx = \int_{-1}^0 (-1)dx + \int_0^1 0dx = [-x]_{-1}^0 + 0 = -(0-(-(-1)))=-1$.
The sum of the integrals is $1+(-1)=0$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{1} (1-x^2)^{3/2} dx$ is:
questions.s:
Let $x=\sin\theta$, so $dx=\cos\theta d\theta$.
The limits change from $0$ to $\pi/2$.
The integral becomes $\int_0^{\pi/2} (1-\sin^2\theta)^{3/2} \cos\theta d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^4\theta d\theta$.
Using Walli's formula, $\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^4\theta d\theta = \frac{(4-1)(4-3)}{4(4-2)} \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3 \cdot 1}{4 \cdot 2} \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{16}$.

questions.q: Let $I = \int_{0}^{10\pi} |\sin x| dx$. The value of $I$ is:

The function $|\sin x|$ is periodic with period $\pi$.
The value of the integral over one period is $\int_0^\pi |\sin x| dx = \int_0^\pi \sin x dx = [-\cos x]_0^\pi = -(-1)-(-1)=2$.
Using the property $\int_0^{nT} f(x) dx = n \int_0^T f(x) dx$ for a periodic function $f(x)$ with period $T$:
$I = \int_{0}^{10\pi} |\sin x| dx = 10 \int_0^\pi |\sin x| dx = 10 \cdot 2 = 20$.

questions.q: The area of the region $\{(x,y): |x-y|\le y\le\sqrt{x}\}$ is A. Then 3A is equal to:

The inequality $|x-y|\le y$ is equivalent to $-y \le x-y \le y$, which simplifies to $x \ge 0$ and $x \le 2y$ (or $y \ge x/2$).
The region is bounded by $y=x/2$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$. [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 
Intersection: $x/2=\sqrt{x} \implies x^2/4=x \implies x=4$.
Area is $A=\int_0^4 (\sqrt{x}-x/2)dx = [\frac{2}{3} x^{3/2}-\frac{x^2}{4}]_0^4 = \frac{16}{3}-4=\frac{4}{3}$. So $3A=4$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{1} (2x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 1)^{1/3} dx$ is:
questions.s:
Let $P(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 1$.
We check for symmetry by evaluating $P(1-x)$.
$P(1-x) = 2(1-x)^3 - 3(1-x)^2 - (1-x) + 1 = -2x^3+3x^2+x-1 = -P(x)$.
Since the integrand $f(x) = (P(x))^{1/3}$ satisfies $f(1-x) = (P(1-x))^{1/3} = (-P(x))^{1/3} = -f(x)$, it is anti-symmetric about $x=1/2$.
Using the property $\int_0^{2a} g(x)dx = 0$ if $g(2a-x)=-g(x)$, with $2a=1$, the integral is 0.

questions.q: The area of the region defined by $|x| + |y| \le \sqrt{2}$ and $x^2+y^2 \ge 1$ is:

The square is rotated by 45 degrees, with vertices at $(\pm\sqrt{2}, 0)$ and $(0, \pm\sqrt{2})$. The area of the square is $\frac{1}{2}d_1 d_2 = \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{2})(2\sqrt{2})=4$.
The area of the unit circle is $\pi$.
The required area is (Area of Square) - (Area of Circle) = $4-\pi$.

questions.q: The area of the major segment of the circle $x^2+y^2=25$ cut by the line $3x+4y=15$ is:

The distance of the line $3x+4y=15$ from the center is $d=3$.
The area of the triangle formed by the chord and radii is 12.
The area of the minor sector is $r^2 \cos^{-1}(d/r) = 25\cos^{-1}(3/5)$.
The area of the minor segment is $25\cos^{-1}(3/5) - 12$.
The area of the major segment is Area(Circle) - Area(Minor Segment) $= 25\pi - (25\cos^{-1}(3/5) - 12)$.

questions.q: Let A be the area of the region $\{(x,y):2y\le x^2+3, y+|x|\le3, y\ge|x-1|\}$. Then 6A is equal to:

The parabola $y \le (x^2+3)/2$ also constrains the region. [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED]

The total area is $A = \int_{-1}^1 (\frac{x^2+3}{2} - (1-x)) dx + \int_1^2 (3-x - (x-1)) dx = \frac{4}{3} + 1 = \frac{7}{3}$. Then $6A = 6(7/3)=14$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\cot x}+\sqrt{\tan x}} dx$ is:
questions.s:
Let $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\cot x}+\sqrt{\tan x}} dx$.
Using King's rule, $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\cot(\pi/2-x)}}{\sqrt{\cot(\pi/2-x)}+\sqrt{\tan(\pi/2-x)}} dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}} dx$.
Adding the two expressions for $I$:
$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\cot x}+\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\cot x}+\sqrt{\tan x}} dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} 1 dx = \pi/2$.
Therefore, $I = \pi/4$.

questions.q: The value of $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^4 x \cos^6 x + x^3 \ln(x^2+1)) dx$ is:

questions.q: Let $F(x) = \int_{1/x}^{x} \frac{\ln t}{1+t^2} dt$ for $x>0$. Then the value of $F(e) + F(2/e)$ is:
questions.s:
We find the derivative of $F(x)$ using the Leibniz rule:
$F'(x) = \frac{\ln x}{1+x^2}(1) - \frac{\ln(1/x)}{1+(1/x)^2}(-\frac{1}{x^2}) = \frac{\ln x}{1+x^2} - \frac{-\ln x}{(x^2+1)/x^2}(-\frac{1}{x^2}) = \frac{\ln x}{1+x^2} - \frac{\ln x}{1+x^2} = 0$.
Since $F'(x)=0$, the function $F(x)$ is a constant for all $x>0$.
We find the constant by evaluating at $x=1$: $F(1) = \int_1^1 (\dots) dt = 0$.
So, $F(x)=0$ for all $x>0$.
Therefore, $F(e) + F(2/e) = 0+0=0$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1+\cos^2 x} dx$ is:
questions.s:
Let $I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1+\cos^2 x} dx$.
Using King's rule, $I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \sin(\pi-x)}{1+\cos^2(\pi-x)} dx = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \sin x}{1+\cos^2 x} dx$.
Adding the two expressions for $I$: $2I = \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi \sin x}{1+\cos^2 x} dx$.
Let $u=\cos x$, $du=-\sin x dx$.
$2I = \pi \int_{1}^{-1} \frac{-du}{1+u^2} = \pi [\tan^{-1}u]_{-1}^1 = \pi(\frac{\pi}{4}-(-\frac{\pi}{4}))=\frac{\pi^2}{2}$. Thus, $I = \frac{\pi^2}{4}$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{1/4}^{3/4} \cos(2\cot^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}) dx$ is:
questions.s:

So, $\cot^{-1}(\tan(\theta/2)) = \pi/2-\theta/2$.
The argument of the cosine becomes $2(\pi/2-\theta/2) = \pi-\theta$.
The integrand is $\cos(\pi-\theta) = -\cos\theta = -x$.
The integral simplifies to $\int_{1/4}^{3/4} (-x) dx = [-\frac{x^2}{2}]_{1/4}^{3/4} = -\frac{1}{2}((\frac{3}{4})^2 - (\frac{1}{4})^2) = -\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9-1}{16}) = -\frac{1}{2}(\frac{8}{16}) = -1/4$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{2+\cos x}$ is:
questions.s:
Using the Weierstrass substitution $t=\tan(x/2)$, we have $\cos x = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $dx=\frac{2dt}{1+t^2}$.
The limits of integration change from $x=0, \pi/2$ to $t=0, 1$.
The integral becomes $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{2dt/(1+t^2)}{2+(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)} = \int_{0}^{1} \frac{2dt}{2(1+t^2)+(1-t^2)} = \int_{0}^{1} \frac{2dt}{t^2+3}$.

The first integrand is an odd function, as it is a ratio of an odd polynomial to an even function ($\cos^2 x$).
The integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval $[-a,a]$ is zero.
The second integral is $\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \sec^2 x dx = [\tan x]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \tan(\pi/4) - \tan(-\pi/4) = 1 - (-1) = 2$.
Thus, the value of the integral is $0+2=2$.

questions.q: If the value of the integral $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+3^x} dx$ is equal to $\frac{\pi}{k}$, find the value of $k$.
questions.s:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+3^x} dx$.
Using the property $\int_{-a}^a f(x)dx = \int_0^a (f(x)+f(-x))dx$, we have:
$f(x)+f(-x) = \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+3^x} + \frac{\cos^2(-x)}{1+3^{-x}} = \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+3^x} + \frac{3^x\cos^2 x}{3^x+1} = \frac{(1+3^x)\cos^2 x}{1+3^x} = \cos^2 x$.
So, the integral becomes $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^2 x dx$.
$I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1+\cos(2x)}{2} dx = \frac{1}{2}\left[x+\frac{\sin(2x)}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+0\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
Comparing this with $\frac{\pi}{k}$, we get $k=4$.

questions.q: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. If the value of the integral $\int_0^2 ([x^2] - [x]^2) dx = a - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$, where $a$ is an integer, find the value of $a$.

• Interval $[0, 1)$: $[x]=0, [x^2]=0$. The integrand is $0-0=0$.
• Interval $[1, \sqrt{2})$: $[x]=1, [x^2]=1$. The integrand is $1-1^2=0$.
 • Interval $[\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$: $[x]=1, [x^2]=2$. The integrand is $2-1^2=1$.
 • Interval $[\sqrt{3}, 2)$: $[x]=1, [x^2]=3$. The integrand is $3-1^2=2$.
The integral is:

$I = 0 + [x]_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} + [2x]_{\sqrt{3}}^2 = (\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}) + (4-2\sqrt{3}) = 4 - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$.
Comparing this with the given form $a - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$, we find that $a=4$.

questions.q: Let A be the area of the region enclosed by the curve $y = \max\{|\sin x|, |\cos x|\}$ and the x-axis between $x=0$ and $x=2\pi$. Then $A^2$ is equal to _______.
questions.s:
The function $f(x) = \max\{|\sin x|, |\cos x|\}$ is periodic with a period of $\frac{\pi}{2}$. We can find the area for one period, from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, and multiply it by 4.
In the interval $[0, \frac{\pi}{4}]$, $|\cos x| \ge |\sin x|$.
In the interval $[\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}]$, $|\sin x| \ge |\cos x|$.
The area over one period is:
$A_{period} = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos x \,dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \sin x \,dx$
$A_{period} = [\sin x]_0^{\pi/4} + [-\cos x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}$
$A_{period} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 0\right) + \left(-0 - (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$.
The total area over $[0, 2\pi]$ is $A = 4 \times A_{period} = 4\sqrt{2}$.
Therefore, $A^2 = (4\sqrt{2})^2 = 32$.

questions.q: Let $\int_{-\infty}^{\alpha} \frac{e^x dx}{\sqrt{1-e^{2x}}} = \frac{\pi}{6}$. Then $e^{\alpha}$ and $e^{-\alpha}$ are the roots of the equation:
questions.s:
To solve the integral, we use the substitution $u=e^x$. Then $du = e^x dx$.
The indefinite integral becomes $\int \frac{du}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} = \sin^{-1}(u) = \sin^{-1}(e^x)$.

Now, we evaluate the definite integral with the given limits:
$I = \left[ \sin^{-1}(e^x) \right]_{-\infty}^{\alpha} = \sin^{-1}(e^\alpha) - \lim_{x\to-\infty}(\sin^{-1}(e^x))$.
As $x \to -\infty$, $e^x \to 0$, so $\lim_{x\to-\infty}(\sin^{-1}(e^x)) = \sin^{-1}(0) = 0$.
The equation becomes: $\sin^{-1}(e^\alpha) - 0 = \frac{\pi}{6}$.
This implies $e^\alpha = \sin(\frac{\pi}{6}) = \frac{1}{2}$.

The roots of the required quadratic equation are $e^\alpha$ and $e^{-\alpha}$.
Root 1: $e^\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$.
Root 2: $e^{-\alpha} = \frac{1}{e^\alpha} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2$.

To form the quadratic equation, we find the sum and product of the roots:
Sum of roots = $\frac{1}{2} + 2 = \frac{5}{2}$.
Product of roots = $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 1$.

The equation is $x^2 - (\text{Sum})x + (\text{Product}) = 0$.
$x^2 - \frac{5}{2}x + 1 = 0$.
Multiplying by 2 to clear the fraction gives the final equation:
$2x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0$.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{50 \cos x}{\cos x + 2 \sin x} dx$ is equal to:
questions.s:
We use the standard form $\int \frac{a \sin x + b \cos x}{c \sin x + d \cos x} dx$.
We express the Numerator as a linear combination of the Denominator and its derivative.
Let Numerator = $A \cdot (\text{Denominator}) + B \cdot (\text{Derivative of Denominator})$.
Here, Numerator is $50\cos x$ and Denominator is $D(x) = \cos x + 2\sin x$.
The derivative of the denominator is $D'(x) = -\sin x + 2\cos x$.
So, we set up the equation:
$50\cos x = A(\cos x + 2\sin x) + B(-\sin x + 2\cos x)$
$50\cos x + 0\sin x = (A+2B)\cos x + (2A-B)\sin x$.
Equating the coefficients of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$:
• $2A - B = 0 \implies B = 2A$
• $A + 2B = 50$
Substituting (1) into (2): $A + 2(2A) = 50 \implies 5A=50 \implies A=10$.
Then $B=2(10)=20$.

The integral becomes:
$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{10(\cos x + 2\sin x) + 20(-\sin x + 2\cos x)}{\cos x + 2\sin x} dx$
$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left( 10 + 20 \frac{-\sin x + 2\cos x}{\cos x + 2\sin x} \right) dx$
$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 10 dx + 20 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{D'(x)}{D(x)} dx$
$I = [10x]_0^{\pi/2} + 20 [\ln|\cos x + 2\sin x|]_0^{\pi/2}$
$I = (10 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} - 0) + 20 \left( \ln|\cos(\pi/2)+2\sin(\pi/2)| - \ln|\cos(0)+2\sin(0)| \right)$
$I = 5\pi + 20(\ln|2| - \ln|1|) = 5\pi + 20\ln 2$.

questions.q: Let the area of the region $\{(x,y): x-2y+4\ge0, x+2y^{2}\ge0, x+4y^{2}\le8, y\ge0\}$ be $\frac{m}{n}$, where m and n are coprime numbers. Then $m+n$ is equal to:
questions.s:
The area is best found by integrating with respect to $y$.
The region is bounded on the right by $x=8-4y^2$ and on the left by $x=-2y^2$ for $y \in [0,1]$ and by $x=2y-4$ for $y \in [1, 3/2]$.
The area integral must be split at the intersection point where $y=1$:
$A = \int_0^1 ((8-4y^2) - (-2y^2)) dy + \int_1^{3/2} ((8-4y^2) - (2y-4)) dy$
$A = \int_0^1 (8-2y^2) dy + \int_1^{3/2} (-4y^2-2y+12) dy$
$A = \left[8y-\frac{2y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 + \left[-\frac{4y^3}{3}-y^2+12y\right]_1^{3/2}$
$A = \left(\frac{22}{3}\right) + \left(\frac{19}{12}\right) = \frac{88+19}{12} = \frac{107}{12}$.
Thus $m=107, n=12$. Their sum $m+n=119$.

questions.q: Let $f(x) = \frac{e^x}{e^x+e^{1-x}}$. If $I_1 = \int_{f(1/4)}^{f(3/4)} x \cos^2(\pi x(1-x)) dx$ and $I_2 = \int_{f(1/4)}^{f(3/4)} \cos^2(\pi x(1-x)) dx$, find the integer value of $100 \cdot \frac{I_1}{I_2}$.
questions.s:
First, analyze the limits of integration. Let $a=f(1/4)$. The upper limit is $b=f(3/4)=f(1-1/4)$.
The function $f(x)$ has the property $f(x)+f(1-x)=1$. So, the limits are $a$ and $b=1-a$. The sum of the limits is $a+b = a+(1-a)=1$.
Let the integrand of $I_1$ be $g(x) = x \cos^2(\pi x(1-x))$. Let $h(x) = \cos^2(\pi x(1-x))$.
Note that the argument of cosine, $\pi x(1-x)$, is symmetric about $x=1/2$, so $h(x)=h(1-x)$.
Using the King's rule on $I_1$:
$I_1 = \int_a^{1-a} x h(x) dx = \int_a^{1-a} (a+(1-a)-x)h(a+(1-a)-x) dx = \int_a^{1-a} (1-x)h(1-x)dx$.
Since $h(1-x)=h(x)$, we have $I_1 = \int_a^{1-a} (1-x)h(x) dx = \int_a^{1-a} h(x)dx - \int_a^{1-a} xh(x)dx = I_2 - I_1$.
This gives $2I_1 = I_2$, so $\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \frac{1}{2}$.
The required value is $100 \cdot \frac{I_1}{I_2} = 100 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 50$.

questions.q: Let $f(x) = \int_{-x}^{x} (t\sin t - t^2\cos t) dt$ and $g(x)=\int_{0}^{x^2}\sqrt{u}\cos(\sqrt{u})du$ be two functions for $x>0$. Then, the value of $\frac{1}{2\pi}\left(f(\pi)+g(\pi)\right)$ is:
questions.s:
We need to evaluate $f(\pi)$ and $g(\pi)$.

1. Analyze f(x):
The integrand of $f(x)$ is $h(t) = t\sin t - t^2\cos t$. Let's check if it's even or odd:
$h(-t) = (-t)\sin(-t) - (-t)^2\cos(-t) = (-t)(-\sin t) - t^2\cos t = t\sin t - t^2\cos t = h(t)$.
Since the integrand is an even function, we can simplify the integral over the symmetric interval $[-x, x]$:
$f(x) = 2\int_{0}^{x} (t\sin t - t^2\cos t) dt$.
So, $f(\pi) = 2\int_{0}^{\pi} (t\sin t - t^2\cos t) dt$.

2. Analyze g(x):
For $g(\pi) = \int_{0}^{\pi^2}\sqrt{u}\cos(\sqrt{u})du$, we use the substitution $u=t^2$.
Then $du=2t dt$, and the limits for $t$ become $\sqrt{0}=0$ and $\sqrt{\pi^2}=\pi$.
$g(\pi) = \int_{0}^{\pi}\sqrt{t^2}\cos(\sqrt{t^2})(2t dt) = \int_{0}^{\pi} t \cos(t) (2t dt) = 2\int_{0}^{\pi} t^2\cos t dt$.

3. Combine and Simplify:
Now we add the two results:
$f(\pi)+g(\pi) = \left(2\int_{0}^{\pi} (t\sin t - t^2\cos t) dt\right) + \left(2\int_{0}^{\pi} t^2\cos t dt\right)$
$f(\pi)+g(\pi) = 2\int_{0}^{\pi} (t\sin t - t^2\cos t + t^2\cos t) dt = 2\int_{0}^{\pi} t\sin t dt$.
We solve this integral using integration by parts: $\int u dv = uv - \int v du$.
Let $u=t$ and $dv=\sin t dt$. Then $du=dt$ and $v=-\cos t$.
$2\int_{0}^{\pi} t\sin t dt = 2 \left( [-t\cos t]_{0}^{\pi} - \int_{0}^{\pi} (-\cos t) dt \right)$
$= 2 \left( (-\pi\cos\pi - 0) + [\sin t]_{0}^{\pi} \right)$
$= 2 \left( (-\pi)(-1) + (0-0) \right) = 2\pi$.

The final required value is $\frac{1}{2\pi}(f(\pi)+g(\pi)) = \frac{1}{2\pi}(2\pi) = 1$.

So I = e^(2x) sin 3x/3 + (2/9) e^(2x) cos 3x - (4/9) I, i.e. (13/9) I = e^(2x)(3 sin 3x + 2 cos 3x)/9. 4. Hence I = e^(2x)(3 sin 3x + 2 cos 3x)/13, so p = 3, q = 2 and p + q = 5. o: ln|3 cos x + 2 sin x| + C
questions.s: 1. Write the numerator as lambda(denominator) + mu(derivative of the denominator). Here the denominator is 3 cos x + 2 sin x and its derivative is -3 sin x + 2 cos x. 2. So 3 sin x + 2 cos x = lambda(3 cos x + 2 sin x) + mu(-3 sin x + 2 cos x). 3. Compare sin x: 3 = 2 lambda - 3 mu. Compare cos x: 2 = 3 lambda + 2 mu. Solving gives mu = -5/13 and lambda = 12/13. 4. Then the integral splits into lambda integral of dx + mu integral of (derivative of denominator)/denominator dx = lambda x + mu ln|denominator|. 5. So the answer is (12/13)x - (5/13) ln|3 cos x + 2 sin x| + C. Differentiating back gives (26 cos x + 39 sin x)/(13(3 cos x + 2 sin x)) = (2 cos x + 3 sin x)/(3 cos x + 2 sin x), as required.

questions.q: Evaluate integral from -1 to 1 of x^5 cos x dx.
questions.s: 1. The interval is symmetric about 0, so test the parity of the integrand. 2. Replacing x by -x: (-x)^5 cos(-x) = -x^5 cos x, so the integrand is odd. 3. By the Jack rule, the definite integral of an odd function from -a to a is 0.

questions.q: Evaluate integral from 0 to 2 of |x - 1| dx.
questions.s: 1. The definition of |x - 1| changes at x = 1, which lies inside the interval, so you are forced to break there. 2. On (0, 1), x - 1 is negative, so |x - 1| = 1 - x; on (1, 2) it is x - 1. 3. integral from 0 to 1 of (1 - x) dx = [x - x^2/2] from 0 to 1 = 1/2, and integral from 1 to 2 of (x - 1) dx = 1/2. 4. Total = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate integral from 0 to 2pi of |cos x| dx.
questions.s: 1. |cos x| is periodic with period pi, so 0 to 2pi is exactly 2 periods. 2. One period: integral from 0 to pi of |cos x| dx. Break at pi/2, where cos x changes sign. 3. integral from 0 to pi/2 of cos x dx = 1 and integral from pi/2 to pi of (-cos x) dx = 1, so one period gives 2. 4. Total = 2 x 2 = 4.

questions.q: Evaluate integral from 0 to 3 of [x] dx, where [.] is the greatest integer function.
questions.s: 1. [x] is a constant on each unit interval and changes definition at x = 1 and x = 2, so break there. 2. On (0, 1), [x] = 0; on (1, 2), [x] = 1; on (2, 3), [x] = 2. 3. I = 0(1) + 1(1) + 2(1) = 3. 4. Whether the break points themselves are included changes nothing, since single points carry no area.

questions.q: Find the value of integral from 0 to 100pi of |cos x| dx.
questions.s: 1. |cos x| has period pi, so the interval 0 to 100pi is exactly 100 periods. 2. One period: integral from 0 to pi of |cos x| dx = 2 (cos is positive on (0, pi/2) and negative on (pi/2, pi), each piece giving 1). 3. Hence the integral is 100 x 2 = 200. Breaking the sign of cos x quadrant by quadrant over 100pi is unnecessary once you use periodicity.

questions.q: If integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^7 x cos^3 x dx = 1/k, find k.
questions.s: 1. Use Wallis, 'come divided by sum', valid because the limits are exactly 0 to pi/2. 2. Top: from 7 take 6.4.2 = 48; from 3 take 2. Product = 96. 3. Bottom: start at 7 + 3 = 10 and step down in twos: 10.8.6.4.2 = 3840. 4. The powers are not both even, so there is no factor pi/2. The integral is 96/3840 = 1/40, so k = 40.

questions.q: If integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^8 x dx = k pi/256, find k.
questions.s: 1. Wallis with m = 8, n = 0. Top: 7.5.3.1 = 105 (there is nothing to take from the zero power). 2. Bottom: start at 8 and step down in twos: 8.6.4.2 = 384. 3. Both powers are even, counting 0 as even, so multiply by pi/2: integral = (105/384)(pi/2) = 105pi/768. 4. 105/768 = 35/256, so the integral is 35pi/256 and k = 35.

questions.q: It is given that integral from 0 to pi of x^4 sin x dx = pi^4 - a pi^2 + b, where a and b are positive integers. Find a + b.
questions.s: 1. Build the reduction formula. With I_n = integral from 0 to pi of x^n sin x dx, integrate by parts twice. 2. First round: I_n = [-x^n cos x] from 0 to pi + n integral from 0 to pi of x^(n-1) cos x dx = pi^n + n integral from 0 to pi of x^(n-1) cos x dx. 3. Second round on that integral: integral from 0 to pi of x^(n-1) cos x dx = [x^(n-1) sin x] from 0 to pi - (n-1) integral from 0 to pi of x^(n-2) sin x dx = -(n-1) I_(n-2). 4. So I_n + n(n - 1) I_(n-2) = pi^n. 5. I_0 = integral from 0 to pi of sin x dx = 2. Then I_2 = pi^2 - 2.1.I_0 = pi^2 - 4, and I_4 = pi^4 - 4.3.I_2 = pi^4 - 12 pi^2 + 48. 6. So a = 12, b = 48 and a + b = 60.

questions.q: If integral from 0 to pi of sin^6 x dx = k pi/16, find k.
questions.s: 1. Wallis needs 0 to pi/2, so bring the limits down first. King on 0 to pi leaves sin^6 x unchanged, so King fails and Queen applies: I = 2 integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^6 x dx. 2. Wallis with m = 6, n = 0: top 5.3.1 = 15, bottom 6.4.2 = 48, both powers even so multiply by pi/2. 3. integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^6 x dx = (15/48)(pi/2) = 5pi/32. 4. Hence I = 2(5pi/32) = 5pi/16 and k = 5.

questions.q: A function f, positive on (0, infinity), satisfies f(x) = integral from 0 to x of dt/f(t) for all x > 0, and f(1) = root 2. Find f(8).
questions.s: 1. There is a variable in a limit of integration, so differentiate first by Newton-Leibniz: f'(x) = 1/f(x). 2. Write y = f(x): dy/dx = 1/y, so y dy = dx and y^2/2 = x + C. 3. The two limits coincide at x = 0, so f(0) = 0, giving C = 0. (The data f(1) = root 2 agrees: 2/2 = 1.) 4. Hence y^2 = 2x and, as f is positive, f(x) = root(2x). So f(8) = root 16 = 4.

questions.q: A continuous function f satisfies integral from sin x to 1 of f(t) dt = 1/(sin x) - 1 for all x in (0, pi/2). Find f(1/root 3).
questions.s: 1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The upper limit 1 is constant and contributes nothing. 2. Left side: -f(sin x) cos x. Right side: d/dx (cosec x - 1) = -cos x/sin^2 x. 3. Cancel -cos x, which is non-zero on (0, pi/2): f(sin x) = 1/sin^2 x. 4. Put sin x = 1/root 3: f(1/root 3) = 1/(1/root 3)^2 = 3.

questions.q: Find the area bounded by y = x^2, the x-axis and the lines x = -1 and x = 2.
questions.s: 1. Sketch: upward parabola with vertex (0, 0), and two vertical lines at x = -1 and x = 2. 2. The curve is above the x-axis throughout, so the vertical stripe is (x^2 - 0) and the limits are x-limits. 3. Area = integral from -1 to 2 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] from -1 to 2 = 8/3 + 1/3 = 3.

questions.q: Find the area between y = sin x and the x-axis for 0 <= x <= pi.
questions.s: 1. On [0, pi] sin x >= 0, so the stripe is (sin x - 0) with no splitting needed. 2. Area = integral from 0 to pi of sin x dx = [-cos x] from 0 to pi = 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.q: Find the area between y = sin x and the x-axis for 0 <= x <= 2 pi, and say why it is not the value of the definite integral.
questions.s: 1. The curve crosses the axis at x = pi, so the legs swap: split there. 2. On [0, pi] the stripe is (sin x - 0); on [pi, 2 pi] it is (0 - sin x). 3. Area = integral from 0 to pi of sin x dx + integral from pi to 2 pi of (-sin x) dx = 2 + 2 = 4. 4. The plain definite integral from 0 to 2 pi is 2 + (-2) = 0, because a definite integral is signed while an area is not.

questions.q: Find the area enclosed by |x| + |y| = 2 without integrating.
questions.s: 1. Replacing x by -x or y by -y leaves the equation unchanged, so it is symmetric about both axes. Draw it in the first quadrant and reflect. 2. In the first quadrant it is x + y = 2, with intercepts (2, 0) and (0, 2). 3. Reflecting gives a square (a rhombus) with vertices (plus or minus 2, 0) and (0, plus or minus 2), so the diagonals are both 4. 4. Area = (1/2) x 4 x 4 = 8, or four triangles of area 2 each.

questions.q: Find the area bounded by y = ln x, the x-axis and the line x = e.
questions.s: 1. y = ln x cuts the x-axis at x = 1 and is positive after that, so the limits are x = 1 to x = e and the stripe is (ln x - 0). 2. Area = integral from 1 to e of ln x dx = [x ln x - x] from 1 to e = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 1.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed between y = |x| - 1 and y = 1 - |x|.
questions.s: 1. y = |x| - 1 is a V with corner (0, -1); y = 1 - |x| is an inverted V with apex (0, 1). They meet where |x| = 1, that is x = plus or minus 1. 2. On (-1, 1) the inverted V is the upper leg, so the stripe length is (1 - |x|) - (|x| - 1) = 2 - 2|x|. 3. Area = integral from -1 to 1 of (2 - 2|x|) dx = 2 x integral from 0 to 1 of (2 - 2x) dx = 2 x 1 = 2. 4. Geometric check: it is a square with diagonals 2 and 2, so the area is (1/2)(2)(2) = 2.

questions.q: Find the area of the region {(x, y) : y^2 <= 2x and y >= x - 4}.
questions.s: 1. y^2 <= 2x is the inside of the rightward parabola y^2 = 2x (test (1, 0): 0 <= 2). y >= x - 4 is the side of the line containing the origin (0 >= -4), that is x <= y + 4. 2. A horizontal stripe runs from x = y^2/2 on the parabola to x = y + 4 on the line, so eliminate x for the y-limits. 3. y^2/2 <= y + 4 gives y^2 - 2y - 8 <= 0, that is (y - 4)(y + 2) <= 0, so -2 <= y <= 4. 4. Area = integral from -2 to 4 of [(y + 4) - y^2/2] dy = [y^2/2 + 4y - y^3/6] from -2 to 4 = (24 - 32/3) - (-6 + 4/3) = 18. 5. Shortcut check: x = y^2/2 has LR = 1/(1/2) = 2, and the root difference is 6, so Area = 6^3/(6 x 2) = 18.

questions.q: Find the total area bounded by the curve y = x^3 - 4x and the x-axis.
questions.s: 1. y = x(x - 2)(x + 2), so the roots are -2, 0 and 2. The cubic is odd, so the two loops have equal area. 2. On (0, 2) the curve is below the axis, so the stripe there is (0 - y). 3. integral from 0 to 2 of (4x - x^3) dx = [2x^2 - x^4/4] from 0 to 2 = 8 - 4 = 4. 4. Total area = 2 x 4 = 8. The plain integral from -2 to 2 would be 0.

questions.q: The line y = mx, with m > 0, cuts the parabola y^2 = 8x and the region enclosed between them has area 4/3. Find m.
questions.s: 1. The parabola is quadratic in y (x = y^2/8), so work with the y-roots. The line gives x = y/m, so y^2/8 = y/m, that is y(y - 8/m) = 0. 2. The root difference is 8/m, and the latus rectum of y^2 = 8x is 8. 3. Area = (8/m)^3/(6 x 8) = 512/(48 m^3) = 32/(3 m^3). 4. Set 32/(3 m^3) = 4/3, so m^3 = 8 and m = 2.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabola y = x^2 - 4 and the line y = -x + 2 is
questions.s: 1. Sketch: y = x^2 - 4 is upward with vertex (0, -4) and roots x = plus or minus 2; the line has intercepts (0, 2) and (2, 0). 2. Intersections: x^2 - 4 = -x + 2, so x^2 + x - 6 = 0, giving x = 2 and x = -3. 3. Between -3 and 2 the line is the upper leg throughout, so one vertical stripe does it: Area = integral from -3 to 2 of [(-x + 2) - (x^2 - 4)] dx = integral of (6 - x - x^2) dx. 4. = [6x - x^2/2 - x^3/3] from -3 to 2 = (22/3) - (-27/2) = 125/6. 5. Shortcut check: the parabola is y = x^2 - 4, so LR = 1/|1| = 1, and the root difference is 5. Area = 5^3/(6 x 1) = 125/6.

questions.q: The area enclosed between the curves y = x^2 and y = -x^2 + 9 is
questions.s: 1. Intersections: x^2 = -x^2 + 9 gives 2x^2 = 9, so x = plus or minus 3/root 2. 2. Over that whole interval the downward parabola is the upper leg and the upward one the lower leg, so no split is needed. 3. Area = integral from -3/root 2 to 3/root 2 of [(-x^2 + 9) - x^2] dx = 2 x integral from 0 to 3/root 2 of (9 - 2x^2) dx. 4. = 2[9x - 2x^3/3] at x = 3/root 2 = 2[27/root 2 - 9/root 2] = 36/root 2 = 18 root 2.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by y = e^x, y = ln x, y = 1/2 and y = 2 is given by
o: integral from 1/2 to 2 of (e^y - ln y) dy
integral from 1/2 to 2 of (ln y - e^y) dy
integral from 1/2 to 2 of (e^x - ln x) dx
integral from ln(1/2) to ln 2 of (e^x - ln x) dx
questions.s: 1. The two bounding lines are horizontal, so take a horizontal stripe: length = x right - x left, limits are y-limits, from y = 1/2 to y = 2. 2. The right leg lies on y = ln x throughout, and y = ln x is the same as x = e^y. 3. The left leg lies on y = e^x throughout, and y = e^x is the same as x = ln y. 4. So the length is e^y - ln y and the area is integral from 1/2 to 2 of (e^y - ln y) dy. (Its value is e^2 - root e + 3/2 - (5/2) ln 2, about 5.51.) 5. Option C is the standard trap: a dx integral cannot be run between y-limits.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by y = ln(x + e), y = e^(-x) and the x-axis is
questions.s: 1. y = ln(x + e) has its vertical asymptote at x = -e, cuts the x-axis at x = 1 - e and passes through (0, 1). y = e^(-x) falls from (0, 1) towards the x-axis. 2. They meet only at (0, 1): for x > 0 the log is above 1 and the exponential below, and for 1 - e < x < 0 the reverse. 3. Horizontal stripes, y from 0 to 1. Right leg on y = e^(-x), so x = ln(1/y) = -ln y. Left leg on y = ln(x + e), so e^y = x + e and x = e^y - e. 4. Area = integral from 0 to 1 of [-ln y - (e^y - e)] dy. Now integral from 0 to 1 of (-ln y) dy = 1 (convergent), and integral from 0 to 1 of (e^y - e) dy = (e - 1) - e = -1. 5. Area = 1 - (-1) = 2. The lecture sets this region up but does not evaluate it.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by y = sin x + cos x and y = |cos x - sin x| for 0 <= x <= pi/2 is
questions.s: 1. sin x + cos x has derivative cos x - sin x, zero at pi/4: it rises from 1 to root 2 at pi/4 and returns to 1. It is the upper curve throughout. 2. cos x - sin x has derivative -(sin x + cos x) < 0 on (0, pi/2), so it decreases from 1 to -1, crossing zero at pi/4. Its modulus is cos x - sin x on [0, pi/4] and sin x - cos x on [pi/4, pi/2]. 3. Split the vertical stripe at pi/4. On [0, pi/4]: (sin x + cos x) - (cos x - sin x) = 2 sin x. On [pi/4, pi/2]: (sin x + cos x) - (sin x - cos x) = 2 cos x. 4. Area = integral from 0 to pi/4 of 2 sin x dx + integral from pi/4 to pi/2 of 2 cos x dx = 2(1 - 1/root 2) + 2(1 - 1/root 2) = 4 - 2 root 2, about 1.17. 5. The class writes down exactly these two integrals but never finishes the arithmetic on air.

questions.q: The area enclosed by the curve 2|x| + 3|y| = 6 is
questions.s: 1. Replacing x by -x and y by -y leaves the equation unchanged, so the curve is symmetric about both axes. Work in the first quadrant and reflect. 2. In the first quadrant the equation is 2x + 3y = 6, a line with x-intercept 3 and y-intercept 2. Keep only the part in that quadrant. 3. Reflecting gives a rhombus with vertices (3, 0), (0, 2), (-3, 0), (0, -2) - four right-angled triangles of legs 3 and 2. 4. Each triangle has area (3 x 2)/2 = 3, so the total is 4 x 3 = 12. No integration is needed anywhere.

questions.q: Let R be the region bounded by y^2 = 4x, the x-axis and the line x = 9, and let S be the rectangle with vertices (0, 0), (9, 0), (9, 6) and (0, 6). Then (area of R)/(area of S) is
questions.s: 1. At x = 9 the parabola gives y^2 = 36, so y = 6 - the rectangle S is exactly the box that encloses the arc. 2. Area of R = integral from 0 to 9 of 2 root x dx = (4/3)(9)^(3/2) = 36. Area of S = 9 x 6 = 54. 3. Ratio = 36/54 = 2/3. 4. This is the general box split: for y^2 = 4ax on 0 <= x <= c the curve cuts the rectangle c by root(4ac) in the ratio 2 : 1, with the 2/3 piece on the side of the parabola's own axis - here the x-axis.

questions.q: The area enclosed between the parabolas y^2 = 8x and x^2 = 12y is
questions.s: 1. Write them as y^2 = 4ax with 4a = 8, so a = 2, and x^2 = 4by with 4b = 12, so b = 3. 2. Two such perpendicular parabolas enclose 16ab/3, which is the product of the two latus recta divided by 3: (8 x 12)/3 = 32. 3. Direct check: they meet at (0, 0) and at x = 4 a^(1/3) b^(2/3), and integral of [root(8x) - x^2/12] dx over that range is 32.

questions.q: If the area of the region bounded by the curves y = ax^2 and x = ay^2, where a > 0, is 1 square unit, then a equals
questions.s: 1. Put both in standard form so the squared term has coefficient 1: y = ax^2 becomes x^2 = (1/a) y, and x = ay^2 becomes y^2 = (1/a) x. 2. So the two latus recta are both 1/a, and the enclosed area is (LR1 x LR2)/3 = (1/a)(1/a)/3 = 1/(3a^2). 3. Set 1/(3a^2) = 1, so a^2 = 1/3 and, since a > 0, a = 1/root 3. 4. Direct check: the curves meet at (0, 0) and (1/a, 1/a), and integral from 0 to 1/a of [root(x/a) - ax^2] dx = 2/(3a^2) - 1/(3a^2) = 1/(3a^2).

questions.q: The area of the region {(x, y) : x^2 + 3y <= 0, y >= -3} is
questions.s: 1. The boundary x^2 + 3y = 0 is x^2 = -3y, a parabola opening downwards with vertex at the origin. 2. Which side? On the boundary the expression is 0; step straight down so y decreases and x^2 + 3y becomes negative. So the region is the inside of the parabola, the side containing (0, -1). 3. y >= -3 cuts it off with a horizontal chord; x^2 = -3(-3) = 9 gives x = plus or minus 3. 4. Area = integral from -3 to 3 of [(-x^2/3) - (-3)] dx = [3x - x^3/9] from -3 to 3 = 6 - (-6) = 12. 5. Box check: the rectangle -3 <= x <= 3, -3 <= y <= 0 has area 18, and the piece on the side of the parabola's axis (the y-axis) is 2/3 of it, which is 12.

questions.q: The area of the region enclosed by y = 2/(1 + x^2) and y = x^2 is
questions.s: 1. y = 2/(1 + x^2) is even, has maximum 2 at x = 0 (where 1 + x^2 is smallest), and tends to 0 at both infinities. y = x^2 is the ordinary upward parabola. 2. Intersections: x^2(1 + x^2) = 2, so x^4 + x^2 - 2 = 0, that is (x^2 + 2)(x^2 - 1) = 0, giving x = plus or minus 1 only. 3. At x = 0 the bell curve is at 2 and the parabola at 0, so the bell curve is the upper leg throughout (-1, 1); no split needed. 4. Area = integral from -1 to 1 of [2/(1 + x^2) - x^2] dx = 2[arctan x] from -1 to 1 - [x^3/3] from -1 to 1 = 2(pi/2) - 2/3 = pi - 2/3.

questions.q: The area enclosed between the parabola y = x^2 - 2x and the line y = x is k/6. Find k.
questions.s: 1. The parabola is quadratic in x, so eliminate y: x^2 - 2x = x, that is x^2 - 3x = 0, giving x = 0 and x = 3. 2. Difference of the roots = 3; the coefficient of x^2 is 1, so LR = 1. 3. Area = 3^3/(6 x 1) = 27/6, so k = 27. 4. Direct check: integral from 0 to 3 of [x - (x^2 - 2x)] dx = integral of (3x - x^2) dx = 27/2 - 9 = 9/2 = 27/6.

questions.q: The line y = mx, with m > 0, cuts the parabola y^2 = 16x and the region enclosed between them has area 2/3. Find m.
questions.s: 1. The parabola is quadratic in y (x = y^2/16), so eliminate x and work with the y-roots. The line gives x = y/m, so y^2/16 = y/m, that is y(y - 16/m) = 0. 2. The roots are y = 0 and y = 16/m, so the difference is 16/m. The latus rectum of y^2 = 16x is 16. 3. Area = (16/m)^3/(6 x 16) = 4096/(96 m^3) = 128/(3 m^3). 4. Set 128/(3 m^3) = 2/3, so m^3 = 64 and m = 4.

questions.q: Find the area of the region bounded by y = |x^2 - 1| and the line y = 3.
questions.s: 1. Draw y = x^2 - 1 and reflect the part below the x-axis upwards: y = |x^2 - 1| is the parabola for |x| >= 1 and the arch 1 - x^2 (height 1 at x = 0) for |x| <= 1. 2. Intersections with y = 3: x^2 - 1 = 3 gives x = plus or minus 2; 1 - x^2 = 3 has no real solution. So the limits are -2 and 2. 3. By symmetry, Area = 2[integral from 0 to 1 of (3 - (1 - x^2)) dx + integral from 1 to 2 of (3 - (x^2 - 1)) dx]. 4. First integral = integral of (2 + x^2) dx = 7/3. Second = integral of (4 - x^2) dx = 16/3 - 11/3 = 5/3. Total = 2(7/3 + 5/3) = 8.

questions.q: Consider the ellipses given by x^2 + 4y^2 = 1 and 4x^2 + y^2 = 1. If alpha is the area of the common region that lies inside both the given ellipses, then the value of cot alpha is ___________.
questions.s: 1. Subtracting the two equations gives 3y^2 - 3x^2 = 0, so the curves meet where y = plus or minus x; then x^2 + 4x^2 = 1 gives the four points (plus or minus 1/root 5, plus or minus 1/root 5). 2. Each ellipse maps to the other under reflection in y = x, so the common region has eight-fold symmetry. Work in the first quadrant and multiply by 4. 3. In the first quadrant the lower boundary is the flatter ellipse x^2 + 4y^2 = 1 (y = root(1 - x^2)/2) for 0 <= x <= 1/root 5, and the steeper one 4x^2 + y^2 = 1 (y = root(1 - 4x^2)) for 1/root 5 <= x <= 1/2. 4. First piece: (1/2) integral from 0 to 1/root 5 of root(1 - x^2) dx = 1/10 + (1/4) arcsin(1/root 5). Second piece: integral from 1/root 5 to 1/2 of root(1 - 4x^2) dx = (1/4)[pi/2 - 2/5 - arcsin(2/root 5)] = (1/4) arcsin(1/root 5) - 1/10, using arcsin(1/root 5) + arcsin(2/root 5) = pi/2. 5. The two 1/10 terms cancel, so the first-quadrant area is (1/2) arcsin(1/root 5) and alpha = 4 x that = 2 arcsin(1/root 5) = 2 arctan(1/2). 6. With t = tan(arctan(1/2)) = 1/2, tan alpha = 2t/(1 - t^2) = 1/(3/4) = 4/3, so cot alpha = 3/4 = 0.75. (Numerically alpha = 0.9273 radians and cot alpha = 0.7500.) 7. Provenance note: the official key for this question could not be read from the source paper file, so the value above is derived here and marked unverified rather than quoted as the official answer.

questions.q: Find the area of the region bounded by the curves y = |x - 1| and y = 3 - |x|.
questions.s: 1. y = |x - 1| is a V with corner (1, 0). y = 3 - |x| is an inverted V with apex (0, 3), cutting the axis at x = plus or minus 3. 2. Intersections: for x >= 1, x - 1 = 3 - x gives (2, 1). For 0 <= x < 1, 1 - x = 3 - x has no solution. For x < 0, 1 - x = 3 + x gives (-1, 2). So the limits are -1 and 2. 3. The inverted V is the upper curve throughout, but both moduli change definition inside the interval, so split at x = 0 and x = 1. 4. On [-1, 0]: (3 + x) - (1 - x) = 2 + 2x, integral = 1. On [0, 1]: (3 - x) - (1 - x) = 2, integral = 2. On [1, 2]: (3 - x) - (x - 1) = 4 - 2x, integral = 1. 5. Total area = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.

flashcards.q: Why must every indefinite integral carry a constant of integration?
flashcards.a: Because a function, that function plus five and that function plus two hundred all have the same derivative. One integrand therefore has infinitely many antiderivatives, differing only by a constant.

flashcards.q: Write the four algebraic formulas of the standard list.
flashcards.a: $$\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C,\quad n \neq -1$$Powers go up by one and divide by the new power, except at the power minus one, which gives the log of the modulus. The two exponentials give themselves back, divided by the log of the base.

flashcards.q: Why do tan, cot, sec and cosec sit in a separate block from sin and cos?
flashcards.a: $$\int \tan x\, dx = \ln|\sec x| + C$$Because the integrals of sine and cosine come straight from derivative knowledge, while the other four do not. Nothing you differentiate gives tan x directly, so they are a separate group proved later by substitution.

flashcards.q: In the inverse-trig pair, which formula carries a factor of one over a and which does not?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a^2 + x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + C$$The inverse sine formula carries no extra factor; the inverse tangent formula does.

flashcards.q: State the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C \;\Rightarrow\; \int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) + C$$In any standard formula you may replace x by a linear expression and the formula stays valid, provided you multiply the answer by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Prove the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\,g(ax+b) + c$$Put the linear expression equal to t, so dx becomes dt over a. The integral becomes one over a times the known integral in t, and converting back gives the rule.

flashcards.q: You have written the log of the modulus of two minus three x. What is still missing?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a + bx} = \frac{1}{b}\ln|a + bx| + C$$The division by the coefficient of x. The coefficient is minus three, so the answer carries a factor of minus one third.

flashcards.q: How do you integrate sin squared x, cos squared x, sin cubed x and cos cubed x?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}, \qquad \cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}$$Reduce each to linear form with the double-angle and triple-angle identities, then integrate term by term, dividing by the coefficient of x each time.

flashcards.q: What are the integrals of tan squared x and cot squared x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \tan^2 x\, dx = \int (\sec^2 x - 1)\, dx = \tan x - x + c$$Tan x minus x, and minus cot x minus x. The stray minus one has to be integrated too, and half the marks sit in that term.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the square of tan x plus cot x?
flashcards.a: $$\int (\sec^2 x + \operatorname{cosec}^2 x)\,dx = \tan x - \cot x + C$$Tan x minus cot x. Expanding gives sec squared x plus cosec squared x, either by the Pythagorean identities or by writing one as sin squared plus cos squared on top.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a sin x plus b cos x sitting in the denominator?
flashcards.a: $$a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(\theta + \phi)$$Take the root of a squared plus b squared common and compress the bracket into a single sine or cosine. What is left is a cosecant or secant with a linear change, so two separate factors appear outside.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over the product of cosine of x minus a and cosine of x minus b?
flashcards.a: $$\int\frac{dx}{\cos(x-a)\cos(x-b)}=\frac{1}{\sin(b-a)}\ln\left|\frac{\cos(x-b)}{\cos(x-a)}\right|+C$$Multiply and divide by the sine of b minus a, and use that sine of a difference over the product of cosines is a difference of tangents.

flashcards.q: What is the first thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(t)\,dt, \quad t = g(x)$$Look for a function whose own derivative is written somewhere in the problem. Call that function t and the integrand collapses to a standard form.

flashcards.q: What is the second thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$x - 5 = t^2 \;\Rightarrow\; dx = 2t\,dt,\quad \sqrt{x-5} = t$$Remove the radical. Put the inside of the root equal to the power that kills it, then differentiate your substitution and convert dx as well.

flashcards.q: What is the third thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\left(x^{n} + 1\right)^{p} = x^{np}\left(1 + x^{-n}\right)^{p}$$Take the highest power of x common from the bracket so that a derivative is manufactured. Remember that the bracket's power travels with whatever you take out.

flashcards.q: Write down the patterns you should integrate by eye.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\, dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$$f prime over f gives the log of the modulus of f; f to the n times f prime gives f to the n plus one over n plus one; f prime over root f gives twice root f; and f times f prime gives f squared over two.

flashcards.q: How many kinds of quadratic actually matter in integration, and what are they?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 + a^2$$Three, once you complete the square: x squared plus a squared, x squared minus a squared, and a squared minus x squared. The fourth shape is negative for every x, so it is never real under a root.

flashcards.q: Write the three formulas for one over the root of a quadratic.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}} \;=\; \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right| + c$$The two with a difference or sum of squares under the root give the log of x plus the root; the one with a squared minus x squared gives the inverse sine of x over a.

flashcards.q: What are the integrals of one over x squared minus a squared and one over a squared minus x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{2a}\,\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right| + C$$Each is a log of a ratio divided by two a, and the two differ only in what sits on top. Remember one of the pair; taking minus one common converts it into the other.

flashcards.q: What is the shortcut for the integral of the root of a quadratic?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sqrt{a^2+x^2}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2+x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\right| + c$$x over two times the same expression, plus or minus a squared over two times the integral of its reciprocal, the sign following the sign in front of a squared. It is a squared over two, not a over two.

flashcards.q: How do you integrate a linear function over a quadratic?
flashcards.a: $$px+q = \frac{p}{2a}\,(2ax+b) + \left(q - \frac{pb}{2a}\right)$$Write the linear as A times the derivative of the quadratic plus B and compare coefficients. The first piece is f prime over f and gives a log; the second is a constant over the quadratic, finished by completing the square.

flashcards.q: A quadratic over a quadratic. What is the first move?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = q(x) + \frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}, \qquad \deg r < \deg Q$$Long division. The derivative of a quadratic is linear, so it can never build an x squared on top; after dividing you are left with a constant plus a linear over a quadratic.

flashcards.q: Only even powers of x appear. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + \frac{a^2}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 + \frac{a^4}{x^2} = t^2 - 2a^2$$Divide the numerator and the denominator by x squared, then look for the derivative of x plus or minus a constant over x on top. Square the substitution on paper to rebuild the denominator in t.

flashcards.q: Which substitution do the two board classics with a fourth power below want?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + \frac{1}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; dt = \left(1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)dx, \quad x^{2} + \frac{1}{x^{2}} = t^{2} - 2$$Read the numerator after dividing by x squared. One minus one over x squared on top means x plus one over x; one plus one over x squared means x minus one over x. The other two are the half-sum and half-difference of these.

flashcards.q: When do you put x equal to one over t?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{(ax+b)\sqrt{cx^{2}+dx+e}}$$When a linear or a quadratic sits outside the root and another quadratic sits under it. After the substitution and a lowest common multiple it usually becomes a linear under a root linear, finished by one more substitution.

flashcards.q: What are the partial-fraction forms for a repeated linear factor and for an irreducible quadratic factor?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{N(x)}{(x-a_1)^2(x-a_2)} = \frac{A}{x-a_1} + \frac{B}{(x-a_1)^2} + \frac{C}{x-a_2}$$A repeated linear factor needs every power from one up to its own, each with a constant on top. A quadratic factor carries a full linear numerator, because the numerator is always one power less than the factor under it.

flashcards.q: What is the fastest way to get the constants in a partial fraction?
flashcards.a: $$x^2+1=A(x-1)(x+3)+B(x+3)+C(x-1)^2$$Clear the denominators and treat the result as an identity valid for every x. Substitute the roots one at a time to kill terms, then compare any one coefficient for the constant that remains.

flashcards.q: The integrand is in x squared throughout. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x^{2}-2}{(x^{2}+2)(2x^{2}+1)} = \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{x^{2}+2} - \frac{5}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2x^{2}+1}$$Do the partial fraction in t equal to x squared as pure algebra, then put x squared back and integrate. Two unknowns instead of four, and you have only rewritten the integrand.

flashcards.q: State integration by parts in words.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,g(x)\,dx = f(x)\int g(x)\,dx \; - \; \int\left[\left(\int g(x)\,dx\right)\frac{d}{dx}f(x)\right]dx$$Stop one function and integrate the other; then a minus sign, a big integral, and inside it the integral you just found times the derivative of the function you stopped.

flashcards.q: Which function do you stop, and which do you integrate?
flashcards.a: $$\int u\,v\,dx = u\int v\,dx - \int\left(\frac{du}{dx}\int v\,dx\right)dx$$Step one: integrate the one whose integral you actually know, so the log and the inverse functions get stopped. Step two, if both are integrable: stop the one whose derivative is easier. Common sense, not ILATE.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of log x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$$x log x minus x. Stop the log, integrate the one to get x, then subtract the integral of x times one over x.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of x times inverse sine of x over the root of one minus x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{x\,\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx=x-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\sin^{-1}x+C$$x minus the root of one minus x squared times the inverse sine of x. Keep x as the first function, because the rest is a ready-made f times f prime.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the square of inverse sine of x?
flashcards.a: $$\int (\sin^{-1}x)^{2}\,dx=x\left[(\sin^{-1}x)^{2}-2\right]+2\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\sin^{-1}x+C$$Substitute inverse sine of x equal to t, so the integral becomes t squared cos t, and two applications of by parts finish it.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of sec cubed x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sec^3 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(\sec x\tan x + \ln\left|\sec x + \tan x\right|\right) + C$$Split it as sec x times sec squared x, always stopping the sec x. The original integral returns, so solve for it like an equation.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of an exponential times a cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}\,(b\sin bx + a\cos bx)}{a^{2}+b^{2}} + C$$Apply by parts twice keeping the same choice both times; the original integral comes back, so shift it to the left and divide. Flip your choice and every step undoes itself.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the log of x plus the root of x squared plus one?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln\!\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\right)dx=x\,\ln\!\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\right)-\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+C$$Stop the log and integrate the one. The derivative of the log is one over the root, which cancels neatly against the x.

flashcards.q: State the exponential formula and its x f prime twin.
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{x}\left(f(x)+f'(x)\right)\,dx = e^{x}f(x)+c$$An exponential multiplied by a function plus its own derivative integrates to the exponential times that function. A function plus x times its derivative integrates to x times the function.

flashcards.q: What is the general version of the exponential f plus f prime formula?
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{g(x)}\left(f(x)\,g'(x) + f'(x)\right)dx = e^{g(x)}f(x) + c$$With an exponential of g of x, the function f must come multiplied by the derivative of g, and the answer carries the same exponential times f.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the log of the log of x plus one over the log of x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \big( f(x) + x\,f'(x) \big)\,dx = x\,f(x) + C$$x times the log of the log of x. Take the log of the log as f; x times its derivative is exactly one over the log of x, so the integrand is f plus x f prime.

flashcards.q: In an integral of a power of tan times a power of sec, how do you choose the substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x \;\Rightarrow\; \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$$The power of the function you call t does not matter. What must be left over after the derivative is an even power of the other one, because the identities convert only even powers. An odd sec power strands a lonely sec x, so there t is sec x.

flashcards.q: For sin cubed x times cos to the fourth x, do you put t equal to sin x or cos x?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$$Cos x. One sine goes into dt and an even power of sine is left, which converts. The power of cosine is then irrelevant, four or fourteen makes no difference.

flashcards.q: Both leftover powers come out odd. What now?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sin^4 x \cos^4 x\, dx = \frac{3x}{128} - \frac{\sin 4x}{128} + \frac{\sin 8x}{1024} + C$$No substitution works, as in sin^4 x cos^4 x and sin^2 x cos^4 x, so fall back on identities: the double angle, one minus cosine and one plus cosine. Count the powers in five seconds and the decision is made.

flashcards.q: The denominator is linear in sin x and cos x. Which substitution?
flashcards.a: $$t=\tan\frac{x}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ dt=\tfrac{1}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{x}{2}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ \sec^{2}\frac{x}{2}\,dx=2\,dt,\qquad dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}$$The tangent of x over two. Everything in this format is half angle, so both sine and cosine carry the secant squared of x over two that becomes dt.

flashcards.q: The denominator is quadratic in sin x and cos x. Which move?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a\sin^2 x + b\sin x\cos x + c\cos^2 x} = \int \frac{\sec^2 x\,dx}{a\tan^2 x + b\tan x + c}$$Divide the numerator and the denominator by cos squared x and work in tan and sec. The secant squared on top is your differential, and the denominator becomes a quadratic in tan x.

flashcards.q: A trigonometric function over a trigonometric function, with nothing cancelling. What is the last resort?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{\lambda D(x) + \mu D'(x) + \gamma}{D(x)}\, dx = \lambda x + \mu \ln|D(x)| + \gamma \int \frac{dx}{D(x)} + C$$Write the numerator as lambda times the denominator plus mu times its derivative, plus gamma if a stray constant is in the way. Compare coefficients, and the answer is lambda x plus mu times the log of the denominator plus the gamma piece.

flashcards.q: Write the statement that turns a derivative result into an integration formula.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big(F(x)\big) = f(x) \iff \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + c$$If the derivative of F is f, then the integral of f is F plus a constant — the same line read in either direction.

flashcards.q: Which single line generates the whole standard list of integrals?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\,F(x) = f(x) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + c$$The flip itself: a derivative result read from right to left is already an integration formula.

flashcards.q: How is the standard list built, and why recall it rather than re-derive it?
flashcards.a: It is built by flipping derivative results — four from the basic derivatives, six more from trigonometry, the rest from logs and inverse trigonometry. Re-deriving an integral in the exam is what keeps integration weak.

flashcards.q: Which functions make up the core list, the one to be memorised like your own phone number?
flashcards.a: Powers, the reciprocal, the two exponentials, sine and cosine, and the two secant and cosecant logs with their half-angle alternatives.

flashcards.q: Write the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C \;\Rightarrow\; \int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) + C$$Any standard formula survives when x is replaced by a linear expression, provided the answer is multiplied by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Why does one rule stretch the whole standard list?
flashcards.a: Because ax plus b may be written wherever x used to sit and the formula still holds, so no second list of formulas is needed for linear arguments.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over a linear expression?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{ax+b} = \frac{1}{a}\ln|ax+b| + C$$The log of the modulus of that expression, divided once by the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Two integrals, two different formulas — what is the same last step in both?
flashcards.a: Dividing once by the coefficient of x. Miss that step and a correct-looking answer scores nothing.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of sin squared x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sin^2 x\, dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + c$$Half of x minus a quarter of sine two x, once the square has been reduced to linear form.

flashcards.q: Why can a power of sine or cosine never be integrated as it stands?
flashcards.a: There is no formula for a power. Convert it to linear form with the double-angle or triple-angle identity first, then integrate term by term with the one over a factor.

flashcards.q: Where does the term in x come from when tan squared x is integrated?
flashcards.a: From the stray minus one. Tan squared x becomes sec squared x minus one, and the minus one has to be integrated too.
