flashcards.a: $$\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^4 x\, dx = \frac{3\cdot 1}{4\cdot 2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{16}$$3 pi over 16, and the fourth power of the cosine gives the same value. Every power here is even, so the pi over 2 factor comes in.

flashcards.q: An odd power appears somewhere. What happens to the pi over 2 factor?
flashcards.a: It disappears completely and the answer is a plain fraction. That factor comes only when every power involved is even.

flashcards.q: State the definite integral as the limit of a sum.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\,f\!\left(\frac{r}{n}\right)=\int_{0}^{1}f(x)\,dx$$The limit of a sum of one over n times f of r over n, with r from 1 to n, is the integral of f from 0 to 1.

flashcards.q: What is the giveaway in a sum-of-series question?
flashcards.a: One spare 1 upon n left sitting outside after everything else has been written in terms of r over n. That spare 1 upon n is the dx.

flashcards.q: Evaluate the limit of the sum of n over n squared plus r squared, with r from 1 to n.
flashcards.a: $$\int_{0}^{1} \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} = \frac{\pi}{4}$$pi/4. Take n squared out below to get one over n times one over 1 plus r over n all squared, so the limit is the integral from 0 to 1 of dx over 1 plus x squared.

flashcards.q: Which integral does the n over n squared plus r squared family become?
flashcards.a: $$\int_{0}^{1} \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} = \frac{\pi}{4}$$The integral from 0 to 1 of dx over 1 plus x squared, whose value is pi over 4.

flashcards.q: What must not survive inside the function once r over n has become x?
flashcards.a: Any stray r or n. If one survives, the common-taking was incomplete, so go back one step.

flashcards.q: How is the rth term read off a spread-out series?
flashcards.a: $$T_r=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{r}\,\left(3\sqrt{r}+4\sqrt{n}\right)^{2}}$$Stack the first few terms: whatever is the same in all of them is frozen and copied untouched, and whatever walks forward is replaced by r.

flashcards.q: What is the last term of a series for?
flashcards.a: Only for telling you where the sum stops. Read the pattern from the first two or three terms, then use the last term to confirm the end.

flashcards.q: A root of x sits alone in the denominator. What do you write?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}}=2\,d\!\left(\sqrt{x}\right)$$dx over the root of x as twice the differential of the root of x. The integral is then a function of the root of x in one line, with no substitution at all.

flashcards.q: The root of n is pulled out of the squared bracket. What has to be tracked?
flashcards.a: The leftover powers. Because the bracket is squared, the root pulled out of it becomes a whole n, and that leftover 1 upon n is the dx.

flashcards.q: How do you fix the limits of integration in a limit-of-a-sum question?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=r_{min}}^{r_{max}} \frac{1}{n} f\!\left(\frac{r}{n}\right) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx, \quad a = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{r_{min}}{n}, \ b = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{r_{max}}{n}$$The lower limit is the limit of r smallest over n, which is 0 in practice, and the upper limit is the limit of r largest over n. So r up to 2n gives 0 to 2, up to 3n gives 0 to 3, and up to n minus 1 still gives 0 to 1.

flashcards.q: How are the limits of integration fixed in a limit-of-a-sum question?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=r_{min}}^{r_{max}} \frac{1}{n} f\!\left(\frac{r}{n}\right) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx, \quad a = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{r_{min}}{n}, \ b = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{r_{max}}{n}$$They are the limits of r over n at the smallest and the largest value of r.

flashcards.q: A limit of a product of n factors is asked. What is the first move?
flashcards.a: $$\ln \lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{2r}{n^{2}} \ln\left(1+\frac{r^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)$$Call the limit lambda and take logs - the product becomes a sum, and the usual one over n times f of r over n rule then applies. There is no direct formula for a product.

flashcards.q: What does a product of n factors become when logs are taken?
flashcards.a: $$\ln \lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{2r}{n^{2}} \ln\left(1+\frac{r^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)$$A sum, which the usual spare 1 upon n times f of r over n rule then handles. A product has no limit formula of its own.

flashcards.q: The sum evaluates to a number. Why is that not the answer?
flashcards.a: Because that number is the log of the limit, not the limit itself. Write the stray constant as a log too, squeeze everything into one single log, and compare.

flashcards.q: What is the length of a vertical segment, in any quadrant?
flashcards.a: $$L = y_{upper} - y_{lower}$$Always y upper minus y lower, taken with signs. Minus 1 minus minus 7 gives 6 exactly as 7 minus 2 gives 5, so the rule never needs a quadrant check.

flashcards.q: Why is a definite integral not the same thing as an area?
flashcards.a: The integral is signed: wherever the curve lies below the axis it contributes a negative amount. An area is always positive, so you split at every crossing and take upper minus lower on each piece.

flashcards.q: Write the vertical stripe formula and say what the limits are.
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{a}^{b}\big(y_{\text{upper}}-y_{\text{lower}}\big)\,dx=\int_{a}^{b}\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx$$Upper curve minus lower curve, integrated in x. Every y has to be written as a function of x, so the limits are x-values taken from the intersections.

flashcards.q: A curve crosses the x-axis at x = c inside your interval. What has to happen to the integral?
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{a}^{c}\big(f(x)-0\big)\,dx+\int_{c}^{b}\big(0-f(x)\big)\,dx$$Split it at c. Up to c the stripe is f of x minus zero; after c the axis is the upper leg, so it is zero minus f of x. Write one integral across the crossing and the two parts cancel.

flashcards.q: Is the case where the x-axis forms one boundary a separate formula to learn?
flashcards.a: No. On the x-axis every y is zero, so putting that zero into upper minus lower reduces the stripe to f of x, or to zero minus f of x where the curve lies below the axis. One subtraction covers every case, and the sign comes out right by itself.

flashcards.q: Write the vertical-stripe set-up for the region between y = x squared, the x-axis and the walls x = minus 1 and x = 2.
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{-1}^{2} \left( x^{2} - 0 \right) dx = \left[ \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right]_{-1}^{2} = 3$$The parabola is the upper boundary and the x-axis the lower one, so the integrand is x squared minus zero across the whole interval. The closing value 3 is this book's arithmetic on that set-up, not a number the lecture produced.

flashcards.q: Is x = minus 1 a horizontal or a vertical boundary, and does this region need splitting at the origin?
flashcards.a: Vertical. x equal to a number is always a vertical line and y equal to a number is always horizontal, so x = minus 1 and x = 2 are the left and right walls. No split is needed, because x squared is never negative and the curve stays above the axis throughout.

flashcards.q: What is the quickest way to sketch a line, with no slope work at all?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1$$Put x equal to zero for the y-intercept and y equal to zero for the x-intercept, then join the two points. You cannot plot the line wrongly that way.

flashcards.q: How do you find where y = x squared minus 4 meets y = minus x plus 2?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 - 4 = -x + 2 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 + x - 6 = 0$$Eliminate y and solve the two equations together. The quadratic factorises and gives x equal to minus 3 and x equal to 2, and putting each x back into the line gives the points minus 3 comma 5 and 2 comma 0.

flashcards.q: Why is it not enough to name the upper curve once and start integrating?
flashcards.a: Because the upper curve can swap inside the interval. Test a point inside first: at the origin the line gives 2 and the parabola gives minus 4, so the line really is on top from minus 3 to 2 and one integral finishes it. Say that sentence out loud and check it holds right across the interval.

flashcards.q: The integral of sin x from zero to twice pi is zero. So what is the area between the curve and the axis there?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \, dx + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} (-\sin x) \, dx = 4$$It is 4, not zero. Split at pi: the stripe is sin x minus zero on the first half and zero minus sin x on the second. The zero is the lecture's point; the 4 is this book's arithmetic.

flashcards.q: How do you write a cubic down from its roots, and what else does the sketch need?
flashcards.a: $$y = x(x-1)(x-2)$$Multiply the factors: a cubic with roots 0, 1 and 2 is x times x minus 1 times x minus 2. Then fix the behaviour at the two ends, and check the sign in each gap by multiplying the signs of the factors.

flashcards.q: What is the least you need in order to sketch a cubic?
flashcards.a: Its three roots and its behaviour at the two ends. Plot the roots, fix the far-left and far-right directions, then read the sign in each gap from the signs of the factors. The sign must flip at every root, so the curve has nowhere else to go.

flashcards.q: For y = x squared and y = minus x squared plus 9 on the region from x = 0 to x = 3, is one integral enough?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \left[ (9 - x^2) - x^2 \right] dx \; + \; \int_{3/\sqrt{2}}^{3} \left[ x^2 - (9 - x^2) \right] dx$$No. The curves cross at x = 3 over root 2, and the legs trade places there: the height is 9 minus 2x squared before the crossing and 2x squared minus 9 after it. One crossing inside the limits means two integrals, so the integral must be broken.

flashcards.q: Where do the two parabolas y = x squared and y = minus x squared plus 9 cross, and what is that point for?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 = -x^2 + 9 \;\Rightarrow\; 2x^2 = 9 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$$Set the two y's equal: 2x squared equals 9, so x is plus or minus 3 over root 2, with y equal to four and a half. That is the break point for the stripe, and it is not the same as x = 3, which is only where the downward parabola meets the axis.

flashcards.q: Over what stretch may the vertical-stripe formula be used as it stands?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_a^b \left( y_{\text{top}} - y_{\text{bottom}} \right) dx$$Only over a stretch where neither boundary changes. Upper curve minus lower curve holds while the same two curves stay above and below; the moment they trade places that stretch ends and a fresh integral begins.

flashcards.q: Write the horizontal stripe formula and say why dy appears.
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{c}^{d} \left( x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}} \right)\, dy$$Right curve minus left curve, integrated in y. The stripe sweeps up and down, so y is what changes, and every x must be written as a function of y, which makes the limits y-values.

flashcards.q: Why does a horizontal stripe carry dy rather than dx?
flashcards.a: Because the stripe sweeps the region by moving up or down, so y is what changes, and the length itself is written in y. The integrand and the differential must speak the same language, so the limits are the smallest and largest y of the region.

flashcards.q: One leg of a horizontal stripe sits on the y-axis. What goes into the formula?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{c}^{d} \left( 0 - g(y) \right) dy$$That leg contributes x equal to zero, so the length is f of y minus zero if the curve is on the right, or zero minus g of y if it is on the left. If the curve crosses the axis inside the region, split at that y and add.

flashcards.q: Write the horizontal-stripe area for a region whose curve crosses the y-axis inside it.
flashcards.a: $$A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \int_{e}^{d} f(y)\, dy + \int_{c}^{e} \left( 0 - g(y) \right) dy$$Two integrals added, split at the switch point. Above it the curve lies to the right, so the stripe is f of y minus zero; below it the curve has gone to the left, so the stripe is zero minus g of y. One formula cannot be carried across the switch point.

flashcards.q: What does a leg of a stripe landing on the y-axis contribute?
flashcards.a: Zero, because on the y-axis x is always zero. The width then collapses to f of y minus zero, or to zero minus g of y when the curve sits on the left, and keeping that order is what makes the answer come out positive.

flashcards.q: The limits of a region are given in y. Which stripe do you take, and what does it give you here?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{1/2}^{2} \left( e^{y} - \ln y \right) dy$$A horizontal one. For the region between the exponential and the logarithm with y running from a half to 2, the stripe is the exponential's x minus the logarithm's x, and the whole region becomes one integral in y; vertical stripes would need splitting. The lecture stops at this set-up, so any number for it is supplied by this book.

flashcards.q: Rewrite y = ln x and y = e to the x with x as the subject.
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln x \iff x = e^{y} \qquad y = e^{x} \iff x = \ln y$$They become x equal to e to the y, and x equal to ln y. Same curves, different packaging, so rewrite rather than re-derive. It is the general logarithm-to-index flip doing the work.

flashcards.q: Which antiderivative do you need the moment a logarithm forms one end of a horizontal stripe?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln y \, dy = y \ln y - y + C$$The integral of ln y, which is y ln y minus y plus a constant. It is wanted as soon as a log boundary has been rewritten as x in terms of y.

flashcards.q: Set up the same parabola-and-line region as a horizontal stripe.
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{y_P}^{y_Q}\left(\frac{2y+3}{4}-\frac{y^{2}}{4}\right)dy$$Write both boundaries as x in terms of y: the line gives x equal to 2y plus 3 all over 4, the parabola gives x equal to y squared over 4. The stripe is the line's x minus the parabola's x, integrated in y between the two intersection points.

flashcards.q: Write the line 4x minus 2y = 3 in the form a horizontal stripe needs.
flashcards.a: $$4x-2y=3\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{2y+3}{4}$$Make x the subject: x equals 2y plus 3, all over 4. A thickness of dy forces every boundary into x as a function of y, and leaving a single x on the wrong side makes the integral impossible to evaluate.

flashcards.q: What is the fastest way to put a line on the page, and what is left once the stripe is set up?
flashcards.a: Two intercepts: put x equal to zero for one point and y equal to zero for the other, then join them, with no slope work. After that the only step left is the two y-coordinates of the intersection points, which become the limits.

flashcards.q: What are the three practice regions in this chapter actually asking for?
flashcards.a: Only the set-up. Plot the region, pick the stripe, write the integral and stop there; the stated reason is that the focus has come off integration. Do not treat any number you have seen for those three as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: How many of this chapter's areas are carried through to a number in the lectures?
flashcards.a: Two. The doubly symmetric modulus region is carried all the way to a number, and so is the exam question on the two-parabola shortcut; each of those values is stated in its own topic. Everywhere else the work stops at the stripe on purpose, the focus having come off integration. Any other value in this kit was supplied by the book, and each topic that carries one says so.

flashcards.q: Which stripe formula closes a region bounded above and below by curves?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( y_{\text{top}} - y_{\text{bottom}} \right) dx$$The vertical one: top curve minus bottom curve, integrated in x between the x-limits. Use the horizontal one instead when the region is closed on its left and right. Fix the stripe direction first and the differential and the limits are then decided for you.

flashcards.q: For the region bounded by y squared = 4x and the line 4x minus 2y minus 3 = 0, how do you get the y-limits?
flashcards.a: $$y^2 - 2y - 3 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (y-3)(y+1) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y = -1,\; 3$$Eliminate x. Push the line's value of 4x into the parabola to get a quadratic in y, factorise it, and read y equal to minus 1 and y equal to 3. Limits always come from the intersections, never from the picture.

flashcards.q: Show the one-step elimination of x for a parabola written as y squared = 4x.
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = 4x, \quad 4x = 2y + 3 \;\Rightarrow\; y^2 = 2y + 3$$The parabola already carries 4x, so push the line's value of 4x in as one block and x disappears at once, leaving a plain quadratic in y. No fractions and no square roots appear on the way.

flashcards.q: Which variable do you eliminate, and where do the limits come from?
flashcards.a: Match the elimination to the variable you will integrate in: integrating in dy means eliminating x. The limits come from the intersections of the two given curves, never from the vertex or from the sketch — here the lower one is minus 1, which sits below the x-axis.

flashcards.q: An area is awkward with a vertical stripe and awkward with a horizontal one. What is the third route?
flashcards.a: $$A=\underbrace{e^{2}\cdot 1}_{\text{rectangle}}-\int_{e}^{e^{2}}\left(\ln x-1\right)dx$$Box the region inside a rectangle whose area you can read off, and subtract the easy stripe integral. Knowing both routes is what lets you pick the shorter one.

flashcards.q: Which antiderivative finishes the rectangle-minus-stripe route on a log boundary?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$$The integral of ln x, which is x ln x minus x plus a constant. It is the only antiderivative the vertical route needs.

flashcards.q: Why learn the rectangle-minus-stripe route at all, when a stripe already works?
flashcards.a: Because some regions are half vertical and half horizontal, and some are a plain box with one small piece bitten out of it. Knowing both routes is what lets you look at a figure and choose the shorter one, and that choice costs nothing.

flashcards.q: Set up the area between y = e to the x, the line y = 1 over e squared and the line x = minus 1.
flashcards.a: $$\int_{-2}^{-1}\left(e^{x}-\frac{1}{e^{2}}\right)dx=\frac{1}{e}-\frac{2}{e^{2}}=\frac{e-2}{e^{2}}$$The curve meets the horizontal line at x = minus 2, so one vertical stripe runs from minus 2 to minus 1 with the exponential on top and the constant below. Keep the answer in e-form rather than going decimal; the closing value here is this book's arithmetic on the lecture's set-up.

flashcards.q: What is the two-second check on an area answer before you believe it?
flashcards.a: Box the region: multiply its x-width by the biggest vertical gap. The answer must come out below that ceiling. Here the box has base 1, from minus 2 to minus 1, so any value above the box's area is wrong on sight.

flashcards.q: Name the four parabola orientations and the tell that gives them away.
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = 4ax,\ a>0$$The right-opening and left-opening ones are squared in y and symmetric about the x-axis; the upward and downward ones are squared in x and symmetric about the y-axis. The variable that is not squared names the axis of symmetry, and its sign says which half-axis the curve opens along.

flashcards.q: Which way does y squared = minus 4ax open, and about which axis is it symmetric?
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = -4ax,\ a>0$$Left, along the negative x-axis, and symmetric about the x-axis. The left side is never negative and 4a is taken positive, so x must be zero or negative; only y is squared, so replacing y by minus y changes nothing.

flashcards.q: Where do x squared = y and x squared = minus y meet the line y = 4x minus 3, and what do the answers tell you?
flashcards.a: $$y = 4x - 3 \Rightarrow x = \frac{y+3}{4}$$The upward parabola gives the points 1 comma 1 and 3 comma 9. The flipped one gives x equal to minus 2 plus or minus root 7. Those surds are the signal that a vertical stripe is the wrong choice here, because a horizontal one keeps one leg on the line throughout.

flashcards.q: An intersection quadratic refuses to factorise. What then?
flashcards.a: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$Stop hunting for factors and use the quadratic formula. For x squared plus 4x minus 3 = 0 it gives x equal to minus 2 plus or minus root 7, and only the root near the origin borders the shaded region. Ugly roots rarely reach the final answer; they only tell you where the picture changes.

flashcards.q: What does replacing y by minus y do to x squared = y, and which stripe suits the region it makes?
flashcards.a: The shape does not change at all: the same parabola is reflected in the x-axis, so it opens downwards with the same vertex and you get a bow-tie around the origin. A horizontal stripe suits the closed patch, because its right leg stays on the line throughout while only the left leg swaps from one parabola to the other.

flashcards.q: Describe the curve y = 2 over 1 plus x squared, and say where it meets y = x squared.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{2}{1+x^2} = x^2 \;\Rightarrow\; x^4 + x^2 - 2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (x^2-1)(x^2+2) = 0$$It is even, so symmetric about the y-axis; the denominator is smallest at the origin, so the maximum value is 2 there; and it tends to zero at both infinities. Against the parabola it meets at x equal to plus or minus 1. Any number quoted for the lens between them is supplied by this book.

flashcards.q: Find the maximum of y = 2 over 1 plus x squared without differentiating.
flashcards.a: $$y = \frac{2}{1+x^2}, \quad 1+x^2 \ge 1 \;\Rightarrow\; 0 < y \le 2$$The numerator is fixed, so y is largest where the denominator is smallest. The denominator is never below 1 and never zero, so y stays positive and reaches its maximum 2 at the origin.

flashcards.q: What is the usable form of the statement that a function is even?
flashcards.a: That the curve is symmetric about the y-axis, so you work out only the right half — the peak, the tail, the shape — and mirror it. The partner statement, that replacing y by minus y changes nothing, is symmetry about the x-axis, and such a relation is not a function of x.

flashcards.q: Run the full checklist on an unfamiliar curve, taking the quotient of x squared minus 1 and x squared plus 1 as the example.
flashcards.a: $$y=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+1}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}$$Even, so symmetric about the y-axis. Roots at plus and minus 1. Value minus 1 at the origin. It tends to 1 at both infinities without reaching it, so that is a horizontal asymptote. The derivative's denominator is a perfect square, so the sign of the derivative is the sign of x: decreasing then increasing. Curvature does not matter, because it never changes the area.

flashcards.q: What does a finite limit at infinity tell you about a curve?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+1}=1$$That the line at that value is a horizontal asymptote. For the quotient of x squared minus 1 and x squared plus 1 the limit at both infinities is 1, and setting the function equal to 1 has no solution, so the curve approaches that line without ever touching it.

flashcards.q: What is the fixed checklist for an unfamiliar curve?
flashcards.a: Even or odd, then the roots, then the value at the origin, then the limit at infinity for an asymptote, then the sign of the first derivative. Five answers and the shape is forced. Here the derivative's denominator is a perfect square, so the sign of the derivative is the sign of x alone.

flashcards.q: How do you draw a translated parabola or a translated V without memorising shift rules?
flashcards.a: $$y = (x - h)^2 + k$$Track the one key point. Set the squared bracket or the modulus to zero, read the y there, and draw the usual shape from that point. For a logarithm the same move gives the vertical asymptote and the domain.

flashcards.q: Where is the vertical asymptote and the domain of a shifted logarithm?
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln(x - a)$$Set the inside to zero for the asymptote and keep it positive for the domain. For a log of x minus a the asymptote stands at x equal to a and the domain is x greater than a. Copying the domain of the plain log is the usual slip.

flashcards.q: How do you avoid the shift-left and shift-right rules altogether?
flashcards.a: Solve instead of remembering. Set whatever sits inside the modulus, the square or the log to zero, put that x back into the whole expression to get the y, and draw the parent shape from that point. Sign mistakes vanish because you solved for x rather than recalling a direction.

flashcards.q: What is the period of f of ax, and how do you use it to draw a rescaled sine?
flashcards.a: $$\text{if period of } f(x) = T \text{ then period of } f(ax) = \frac{T}{|a|}$$The old period divided by the modulus of a. So keep the sine shape untouched and divide every marked x-value by the modulus of a: halve them for sin 2x, double them for sin of x over 2, multiply by two-thirds for sin of 3x over 2. Rescale the numbers, never squash the picture.

flashcards.q: What verifies a rescaled sine graph once you have relabelled it?
flashcards.a: One complete wave must end exactly at the period you computed. Divide every marked x-value by the modulus of a, then check the closing point: if it does not match the period, you divided the wrong way round.

flashcards.q: How do you draw f of mod x from f of x?
flashcards.a: $$f(|x|)=\begin{cases} f(x), & x\ge 0 \\ f(-x), & x<0 \end{cases}$$Throw away the part left of the y-axis, keep the part to the right, and mirror that right half across the y-axis. The function is even by construction, so the two halves have to agree.

flashcards.q: What is the one-line check that f of mod x must be even?
flashcards.a: $$f(|-x|)=f(|x|)$$The modulus of minus x equals the modulus of x, so the value at minus x is the same as the value at x. An even function can only be symmetric about the y-axis, and that single fact draws the curve for you.

flashcards.q: What happens to the original negative-x part of the graph when you draw f of mod x?
flashcards.a: It is discarded. Keep the graph only for x at least zero, where the modulus does nothing, then mirror that right half across the y-axis. Leaving the old left branch in place gives a graph with two different left halves.

flashcards.q: How do you draw the modulus of f of x?
flashcards.a: $$|f(x)| = \begin{cases} f(x), & f(x) \ge 0 \\ -f(x), & f(x) < 0 \end{cases}$$Keep every piece already above the x-axis as it is, and reflect every piece below the axis up above it. Nothing may stay negative, so a drawing that dips below the axis is wrong.

flashcards.q: What is the one-line check on a finished drawing of the modulus of f of x?
flashcards.a: $$|f(x)| \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } x$$No part of it may sit below the x-axis, because a modulus is never negative. The points where the original graph already touched the axis do not move, and those become the sharp corners.

flashcards.q: In the modulus of f of x, what happens to the part that was below the axis?
flashcards.a: It is reflected straight up, not erased. The x-axis acts as a mirror: everything already above it stays untouched and nothing is shifted sideways. The modulus sits on the output, which is why the mirror is the x-axis and not the y-axis.

flashcards.q: Why is mod y = f of x not a function, and how do you draw it?
flashcards.a: $$|y| = f(x) \iff y = \pm f(x), \quad f(x) \ge 0$$One x gives two y-values, plus and minus f of x. To draw it, delete every x where f of x is negative, because a modulus cannot equal a negative number, then keep what is left and mirror it across the x-axis, since replacing y by minus y changes nothing.

flashcards.q: Why is mod y = f of x symmetric about the x-axis?
flashcards.a: $$|-y| = |y|$$Because replacing y by minus y leaves the equation unchanged. So whatever is drawn above the axis appears identically below it, and every point you keep comes with its mirror image.

flashcards.q: In which two steps, and in which order, do you draw mod y = f of x?
flashcards.a: Erase first, then mirror. Erase every part of the curve lying below the x-axis, because a modulus cannot match a negative value and there is no graph there at all. Then reflect what survives about the x-axis. Mirror first and you reflect a piece that should not exist.

flashcards.q: Set up the area bounded by y = ln of x plus e, the curve y = e to the minus x and the x-axis. Does the lecture finish it?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{1}\left(x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}}\right)dy = \int_{0}^{1}\left(-\ln y - e^{y} + e\right)dy$$No. The asymptote is fixed first, the log is inverted to x equal to e to the y minus e, and the other curve is written as minus ln y. Horizontal strips from y = 0 to y = 1 then give a single integral, and the lecture goes no further than that integral. The value 2 often quoted for it is supplied by this book, not produced in the lecture.

flashcards.q: Invert y = ln of x plus e, and say where its asymptote stands.
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln(x+e) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; x = e^{y} - e$$It becomes x equal to e to the y minus e. The asymptote follows the inside of the log: set x plus e to zero and it stands at x equal to minus e, not at the origin. Setting the inside to 1 instead gives the x-intercept at x equal to 1 minus e.

flashcards.q: How does sin x plus cos x behave between zero and a right angle, and how do you open the companion modulus?
flashcards.a: $$|\cos x - \sin x| = \begin{cases} \cos x - \sin x, & 0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{4} \\ \sin x - \cos x, & \frac{\pi}{4} \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2} \end{cases}$$Differentiate: the derivative is cos x minus sin x, zero at a quarter of pi, positive before and negative after, so the curve rises from 1 to a peak of root 2 and comes back to 1. The companion curve cos x minus sin x decreases across the whole interval, so it crosses the axis once, and the modulus opens as cos x minus sin x before the corner and sin x minus cos x after it.

flashcards.q: How do you place the peak of sin x plus cos x between zero and a right angle?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x + \cos x) = \cos x - \sin x$$Differentiate rather than guess. The derivative is cos x minus sin x, which vanishes where tan x equals 1, so the only critical point inside the interval is a quarter of pi. The derivative is positive before it and negative after it, so the curve rises from 1 to root 2 and falls back to 1.

flashcards.q: Why must cos x minus sin x be drawn before the modulus is put on it?
flashcards.a: Because the modulus has to be opened piecewise, and that needs the crossing. Its derivative is minus the sum of sin x and cos x, which is negative across the whole interval, so the curve falls steadily from 1 to minus 1 and crosses the axis exactly once. Only then do you lift the negative piece.

flashcards.q: Set up the area between sin x plus cos x and the modulus of cos x minus sin x. How much of this comes from the lecture?
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}2\sin x\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}2\cos x\,dx$$The two integrals come from the lecture: split at a quarter of pi, with stripe height 2 sin x before it and 2 cos x after it. The closing number does not. Treat 4 minus 2 root 2 as this book's figure, supplied here rather than produced in the lecture, and do not quote it as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: What do the lectures for this chapter leave unfinished?
flashcards.a: Two regions are set up and never evaluated: the log pair and the trigonometric pair. The circle-and-parabola area is only quoted rather than worked, and most of a lettered run of plotting-region questions is left undone. Treat every value attached to those as supplied by this book, not as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: Open the modulus of cos x minus sin x on zero to a right angle.
flashcards.a: $$|\cos x-\sin x|=\begin{cases}\cos x-\sin x, & 0\le x\le \pi/4\\ \sin x-\cos x, & \pi/4\le x\le \pi/2\end{cases}$$Ask which term is bigger on each piece and write that one first. Before a quarter of pi cos x is bigger, so it opens as cos x minus sin x; after it sin x is bigger, so it opens as sin x minus cos x. The corner sits where the two are equal.

flashcards.q: Find the area enclosed by 2 mod x plus 3 mod y = 6 without integrating.
flashcards.a: $$\text{Area} = 4 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 2 = 12$$It is 12, and this one really is a lectured result. The relation is unchanged when x or y changes sign, so it is symmetric about both axes: draw the line in the first quadrant only, from intercepts 3 and 2, take that right triangle's area of 3, and multiply by 4.

flashcards.q: When may you work one quadrant and multiply by 4?
flashcards.a: $$\text{Area}_{\text{total}} = 4 \times \text{Area in first quadrant}$$The moment both minus x and minus y leave the relation unchanged. A modulus in both variables does exactly that, so whatever shape appears in the first quadrant repeats in the other three.

flashcards.q: Why is there no integration in this region at all?
flashcards.a: Because the boundary is made only of straight lines. Once symmetry reduces the work to the first quadrant, the piece there is a right triangle read off the two intercepts, and the four copies make a rhombus. Checking symmetry and reading the shape is the whole method.

flashcards.q: Give the two ways of deciding which side of a boundary an inequality shades.
flashcards.a: $$P(x_0, y_0) \to P'(x_0, y_0 + h),\quad h > 0$$Test a convenient point, usually the origin: the side containing a point that satisfies the inequality is the shaded one. Or step off the boundary, where the expression equals the constant exactly, straight upwards so that y increases, and see whether the expression grows or shrinks. The second test is claimed for ellipses and hyperbolas too, though no worked example on either appears.

flashcards.q: Which side of the line 2x plus 3y = 6 does the inequality 2x plus 3y at most 6 shade?
flashcards.a: $$2x + 3y \le 6$$The side below it, which is the side containing the origin. Putting the origin in gives 0, which is at most 6, so that settles it; and stepping up from a point on the line makes the expression grow past 6, so up is the wrong direction.

flashcards.q: When does the origin test fail you, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: It fails when the boundary passes through the origin, because there is then no side to read. Stand on the curve instead, where the expression equals its constant exactly, step straight up so that y increases, and see whether the value grows: if it grows and you wanted at most, come down.

flashcards.q: Which region does x squared plus 3y at most zero describe?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 + 3y = 0 \iff x^2 = -3y$$The inside of the downward parabola whose equation is x squared equal to minus 3y. Step down from a point on the boundary and the expression becomes negative, so the shaded side is the one containing the point 0 comma minus 1.

flashcards.q: Write x squared plus 3y = 0 in y-form and say which way it opens.
flashcards.a: $$y = -\frac{x^2}{3}$$It is y equal to minus x squared over 3: a downward parabola with its vertex at the origin. Rearranging into that form first is what stops it being drawn opening upwards.

flashcards.q: Which standard antiderivative does a circular leg of a strip always need?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sqrt{a^{2}-y^{2}}\,dy = \frac{y}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-y^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{y}{a} + C$$The standard result for the root of a constant minus a square, which gives half the variable times the root plus an inverse sine term. Worth noting that this is never derived or used anywhere else in this chapter, so you are learning it here.

flashcards.q: Set up the area common to the circle of radius 2 and the parabola y squared = 3x. What should you be careful about?
flashcards.a: $$A = 2\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\left(\sqrt{4-y^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{3}\right)dy$$Take a horizontal strip: the right leg is the circle, the left leg the parabola, y runs from zero to root 3, and you double for symmetry about the x-axis. The care is about provenance. The lecture goes only as far as that strip set-up, the circular antiderivative it needs is never taught in this chapter, and the closing value is supplied by this book rather than produced in the lecture.

flashcards.q: What is missing from this chapter altogether, that you must get from practice rather than the lectures?
flashcards.a: Any area needing a circular integral, and so every circle region; the area of an ellipse and the common area of two ellipses, which both of this chapter's genuine past-paper items require; a line dividing a region in a given ratio; area as a parameter to be maximised or minimised; area against a curve's own tangent; regions built from the greater or smaller of two functions; and regions using the greatest-integer or fractional-part functions. No past-paper question is worked through anywhere in the lectures.

flashcards.q: State the parabola-in-its-box split, the first of the three shortcuts.
flashcards.a: $$A = \frac{2}{3}A_{\text{rect}}, \qquad A_{\text{outside}} = \frac{1}{3}A_{\text{rect}}$$For the standard right-opening parabola cut by a vertical line, the piece on one side of the axis is four-thirds root a times the cut abscissa to the three-halves, and twice that for both halves. The circumscribing rectangle is the abscissa by the full chord, and the parabola splits it two-thirds to one-third, with the two-thirds piece on the parabola's own axis side. That lets you skip the integration.

flashcards.q: Why do the three parabola shortcuts sit at the end of this chapter rather than inside it?
flashcards.a: Because that is where the chapter's own ordering puts them. The three shortcuts come after the early-section questions they would have shortened, alongside the leftover circle-and-parabola region. They belong to Area Under Curves, so keep them here and use them on those earlier questions too.

flashcards.q: What area do two perpendicular standard parabolas enclose?
flashcards.a: $$A = \frac{(\text{LR}_1)(\text{LR}_2)}{3} = \frac{(4a)(4b)}{3}$$16ab over 3, which is the product of their two latus recta divided by 3, since the latus recta are 4a and 4b. Remember it in the latus-rectum form, because that is what you can read off an exam question.

flashcards.q: In y squared = 8x, what is a?
flashcards.a: 2. Compare with y squared = 4ax first, so 4a equals 8 and a is 2. Reading the coefficient itself as a is the usual slip, and the same care applies to the partner parabola: x squared = 12y gives 4b equal to 12, so b is 3.

flashcards.q: Two parabolas, the coefficient of the squared term being a in each, enclose an area of 1. Find a.
flashcards.a: $$ax^2 = y \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 = \frac{1}{a}y, \qquad ay^2 = x \;\Rightarrow\; y^2 = \frac{1}{a}x$$a is 1 over root 3. Standardise first, so each parabola has the squared variable's coefficient equal to 1 and each latus rectum is 1 over a. The shortcut then gives 1 over 3a squared, set that to 1, and a squared is a third. This is the second of only two numbers the lectures actually produce.

flashcards.q: Write the two-parabola shortcut in the form you apply in an exam.
flashcards.a: $$\text{Area} = \frac{LR_1 \times LR_2}{3}$$Multiply the two latus recta and divide by 3. Put both parabolas in standard form first, so the coefficient of the squared variable is 1, then read each latus rectum off. Check the direction of the 3 on a known pair: two latus recta of 4 each give 16 over 3, so it is a division.

flashcards.q: Your answer to a shortcut question is 1 over root 3, and the options do not show it. What now?
flashcards.a: Rationalise your own answer before deciding it is absent. The same number can be printed as root 3 over 3, so convert it and look again.

flashcards.q: State the chord-cut shortcut for a parabola.
flashcards.a: $$A = \frac{|x_2-x_1|^3}{6\,\text{(LR)}}$$The area between a parabola and a chord is the cubed difference of the roots divided by six times the latus rectum. It stays valid for a shifted parabola, so you do not have to move anything back to standard position.

flashcards.q: How do you read the latus rectum straight off a shifted parabola?
flashcards.a: $$y = ax^2+bx+c \;\Rightarrow\; \text{LR} = \frac{1}{|a|}$$A parabola is quadratic in exactly one variable. Write it that way and the latus rectum is one over the modulus of the leading coefficient. Shifting cannot change it, because only the linear and constant terms move.

flashcards.q: In the chord shortcut, do you take the difference of the x-roots or of the y-roots?
flashcards.a: $$A=\frac{(\Delta)^3}{6\ell},\qquad \ell=\frac{1}{|a|}$$Follow the parabola. If it is quadratic in x, so it reads y as a function of x, eliminate y and use the difference of the x-roots. If it is quadratic in y, so it reads x as a function of y, eliminate x and use the difference of the y-roots.

flashcards.q: The quadratic from the chord has horrible surd roots. Now what?
flashcards.a: $$\Delta=|x_2-x_1|=\frac{\sqrt{D}}{|a|},\qquad D=b^2-4ac$$Nothing changes. You never need the roots themselves, only their difference, and that is the root of the discriminant over the modulus of the leading coefficient. Cube it and divide by six times the latus rectum.

flashcards.q: The parabola is quadratic in y. Which difference goes into the chord shortcut, and how do you get it?
flashcards.a: $$\Delta=|y_2-y_1|=\frac{\sqrt{D}}{|a|}$$The difference of the y-roots, obtained without solving: root of the discriminant over the modulus of the leading coefficient. Eliminate x so the quadratic comes out in y, then cube that difference and divide by six times the latus rectum. Check the discriminant first — a negative one means the line never cuts the parabola, so there is no region to find.

flashcards.q: Does it matter whether you read the latus rectum off the parabola or off the final quadratic?
flashcards.a: No, it is the same number. Eliminating the other variable removes linear and constant terms but never touches the coefficient of the squared variable, so the modulus of that leading coefficient — and the latus rectum read from it — does not move.

mistakes.m: Leaving out + c.
mistakes.fix: A constant dies on differentiating, so an indefinite integral is a whole family — write + c in the same stroke as the answer, every single time.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Forgetting the 1/a factor when x is replaced by ax + b, or losing the minus sign when a is negative.
mistakes.fix: After applying any formula, immediately divide by the coefficient of x and carry its sign: ∫dx/(2 − 3x) = −(1/3)ln|2 − 3x| + c.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Writing ∫dx/x = ln x without the modulus, and the same inside every log answer.
mistakes.fix: It is ln|x| + c. Keep the modulus on ln|f|, ln|sec x + tan x|, ln|x + √(quadratic)| — marks are cut for the bare log.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Expecting tan x, cot x, sec x, cosec x to integrate as directly as sin x and cos x.
mistakes.fix: Those four are not derivative-reversals; they come from separate work (sec x needs the sec x + tan x manipulation). Learn those four results as their own line on the sheet.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Substituting t but not converting dx, or finishing the answer in t.
mistakes.fix: Every substitution has two halves — the function and its differential. Write dt = f′(x)dx on the same line, and put x back at the end.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Mixing up the nine quadratic formulas — sin⁻¹ used for x² − a², or 1/(x² − a²) given a tan⁻¹ answer.
mistakes.fix: Decide the shape first (x² + a², x² − a², a² − x²), then read the matching formula. Remember the pairs: 1/(x² − a²) → (1/2a)ln|(x − a)/(x + a)|, 1/(a² − x²) → (1/2a)ln|(a + x)/(a − x)|.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Doing partial fractions on an improper fraction, or using the wrong form for a repeated or quadratic factor.
mistakes.fix: Divide first until the top is of lower degree. Then: repeated factor needs B/(x − a) and C/(x − a)², a quadratic factor needs px + q on top, a linear factor only a constant — always one power less above than below.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
In by parts, losing the minus sign on the second integral or stopping the wrong function.
mistakes.fix: The formula is (stopped)·(integral of other) − ∫(integral of other)·(derivative of stopped). If the derivative of your stopped function is getting worse, you stopped the wrong one — swap.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Reaching for by parts when a substitution would clear the question first.
mistakes.fix: ∫cos√x dx is not a by-parts question until √x = t makes it ∫2t cos t dt. Always substitute away the awkward inside before you split a product.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Integrating a degree angle as if it were radians, like ∫cos(x°)dx.
mistakes.fix: Convert inside first: x° = πx/180, so ∫cos(x°)dx = (180/π)sin(πx/180) + c.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Substituting t = ln x or t = sin x and keeping the old limits.
mistakes.fix: The limits belong to the variable. Change the variable, change the limits — a ln x range of 0 to 1 is an x range of 1 to e.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Integrating a mod or a greatest-integer function in one shot.
mistakes.fix: Wherever the definition changes inside the interval, breaking is a compulsion, not a choice. Find every break point first, open the function on each piece, then integrate.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Using a substitution that blows up inside the interval — t = tan x across π/2, t = 1/x across 0.
mistakes.fix: Check whether the new variable stays finite on the whole interval. If not, break at that point and do the two halves separately.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Writing F(b) − F(a) when the antiderivative is undefined at a limit.
mistakes.fix: Take the one-sided limiting value there. If that limit is infinite, the integral diverges — say so instead of writing a number.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Rejecting a negative answer because 'area cannot be negative'.
mistakes.fix: A definite integral is the algebraic sum of areas: above the axis adds, below subtracts. It is allowed to be positive, zero or negative.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Halving the upper limit with Queen whenever the interval looks like 0 to 2a.
mistakes.fix: Queen needs both conditions: the lower limit must be 0 and King must genuinely change nothing. Verify f(2a − x) = f(x) before you halve.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Dropping the derivative of the limit in Newton–Leibniz.
mistakes.fix: Every limit brings its own derivative: f(upper)·(upper)′ − f(lower)·(lower)′. With an upper limit of x², the factor 2x must be there.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Applying Wallis to limits that are not 0 to π/2.
mistakes.fix: Wallis is only for 0 to π/2. Use King and Queen to bring the interval down first, then apply the shortcut.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
In a limit-of-a-sum, forgetting the spare 1/n or taking the upper limit as 1 out of habit.
mistakes.fix: Arrange the term as (1/n)·f(r/n). The lower limit is almost always 0 and the upper limit is lim rₘₐₓ/n — so 2n gives 2, 3n gives 3, n−1 still gives 1.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Carrying +C into a definite integral, or writing ∫ 0 dx = C over an interval.
mistakes.fix: In F(b) − F(a) the constant always cancels, so never write it. The definite integral of 0 over any interval is 0.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Writing area = ∫f(x) dx when part of the curve is below the x-axis, so the pieces cancel.
mistakes.fix: Find the roots in the interval first, split there, and take 0 − f(x) on every piece where the curve is below the axis. That is why ∫sin x dx from 0 to 2π is 0 but the area is 4.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Taking a horizontal stripe but still writing dx, or keeping y-limits on a dx integral.
mistakes.fix: A horizontal stripe is x(right) − x(left), both written as functions of y, integrated dy between y-limits. If any x is still sitting inside the bracket, you have not finished converting.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Using one integral when the boundary curve changes somewhere inside the region.
mistakes.fix: Mark every intersection point and every corner, and break the integral at each one. Each sub-integral must have the same pair of boundaries from its start to its end.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Guessing which curve is on top and getting a negative area.
mistakes.fix: Put one convenient x from inside the interval into both curves and compare the two numbers. A negative answer means you swapped the legs, not that the area is negative.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Finding the x-coordinates of the intersections and then using them as y-limits.
mistakes.fix: For dy integration eliminate x, not y. Substitute the line's 4x into y² = 4x and factorise the quadratic in y to get the y-limits directly.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Applying 16ab/3 straight to something like 3y² = 16x without standardising it.
mistakes.fix: Divide until the coefficient of y² and of x² is 1, then match y² = 4ax and x² = 4by to read a and b. Here a = b = 4/3, not 16/3.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Cubing the wrong difference in the (Δ)³ / (6 × LR) formula.
mistakes.fix: Cube the difference of the variable that appears squared. y² = 4ax is quadratic in y, so use Δy; x² = 4ay is quadratic in x, so use Δx.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Treating |y| = f(x) as a function and drawing it even where f(x) is negative.
mistakes.fix: |y| = f(x) gives two y-values for one x, so it is not a function. Draw y = f(x) where f(x) ≥ 0, mirror it below the x-axis, and leave a gap wherever f(x) < 0.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Mixing up y = f(|x|) and y = |f(x)|.
mistakes.fix: f(|x|) is even: keep the x ≥ 0 part and mirror it across the y-axis, throwing the old left half away. |f(x)| keeps the x-values and flips whatever was below the x-axis up above it.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Shading the wrong side of a curve for an inequality, so the whole area is wrong before any integration starts.
mistakes.fix: Put (0, 0) in: if it satisfies the inequality, shade the side containing the origin. If the curve passes through the origin, take any point P on the curve, move to P' just above it, and see whether the expression grows or falls.
